abstract:
  "The Diffusion Decision Model (DDM) decomposes response time and accuracy data from speeded decision-making tasks into cognitive process parameters, such as the rate of evidence accumulation, response caution, and non-decision time. Despite its success over the past decades, DDM analysis often still use step-wise analysis approaches that can lead to inappropriate inferences and over-parametrization. The bmm R package provides easy and accessible implementations of one-step Bayesian hierarchical estimation of DDM parameters, including the EZ-Diffusion Model (summary-statistic approach), the Censored-Shifted Wald (a faster trial-level approximation), and full DDM likelihood estimation via the Wiener first-passage time distribution. This tutorial demonstrates how to apply all three within a one-step Bayesian hierarchical framework. In addition, it covers data preprocessing and contaminant handling to achieve robust parameter estimation. Across four examples, the tutorial shows how to apply the different estimation approaches to the classic lexical decision dataset from Wagenmakers et al. (2008). Results from the different methods are compared to evaluate where they agree and where they diverge. Complete R scripts accompany each tutorial. After working through the examples, you will understand what to look out for during preprocessing of RT data, you will be able to select the appropriate estimation approach for your research question, fit it using bmm, and interpret the results in cognitive terms."

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| eval: true
pacman::p_load(here, bmm, brms, rtdists, tidyverse, tidybayes, patchwork)
source(here("functions", "clean_plot.R"))

# Load fitted models for real data
fit_acc_ezdm      <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm     <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_cswald_simple <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple.rds"))
fit_cswald_resp   <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_ddm_acc       <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc.rds"))
fit_ddm_resp      <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp.rds"))
fit_acc_ezdm_freq <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc_freq.rds"))
fit_resp_ezdm_freq <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp_freq.rds"))

# Load simulated models for appendix
fit_ezdm_3par    <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ezdm_3par.rds"))
fit_cswald_crisk <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_cswald_crisk.rds"))
fit_ddm          <- readRDS(here("output", "fit_ddm.rds"))
true_params      <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters.csv"),
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
true_params_subject <- read_csv(here("data", "true_parameters_subject.csv"),
                                 show_col_types = FALSE)

# Cached prepared datasets, used to display the required data formats
data_accuracy_clean <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_accuracy_triallevel.csv"),
                                show_col_types = FALSE)
data_acc_ezdm <- read_csv(here("data", "lexical_accuracy_ezdm3par.csv"),
                          show_col_types = FALSE)

# --- Extract inline reporting values ---

# Helper: format estimate with 95% CrI
fmt_est <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  sprintf("%.*f [%.*f, %.*f]", digits, x["Estimate"],
          digits, x["Q2.5"], digits, x["Q97.5"])
}

# Tutorial 1: EZDM 3par (accuracy-coded)
fe_t1 <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
t1_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_acc_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t1_ess  <- min(summary(fit_acc_ezdm)$fixed[, "Bulk_ESS"], na.rm = TRUE)
t1_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catword", ])
t1_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t1["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t1_bound_speed   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_bound_acc     <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t1_ndt           <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t1["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
# Equality hypotheses: Evid.Ratio is the Savage-Dickey BF *for* equality;
# its inverse quantifies the evidence against equality (reported as BF in text)
t1_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword")
t1_bf_drift  <- 1 / t1_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t1_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed")
t1_bf_bound  <- 1 / t1_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 2: EZDM 4par (response-coded)
fe_t2 <- fixef(fit_resp_ezdm)
t2_rhat <- max(brms::rhat(fit_resp_ezdm), na.rm = TRUE)
t2_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catword", ])
t2_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t2["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t2_zr_speed <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_acc   <- round(plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]), 3)
t2_zr_speed_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionspeed", "Q97.5"]))
t2_zr_acc_ci <- sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]",
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Estimate"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q2.5"]),
  plogis(fe_t2["zr_conditionaccuracy", "Q97.5"]))

# Tutorial 2: Hypothesis tests
t2_hyp_drift_word <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catword = 0")
t2_bf_drift_word  <- 1 / t2_hyp_drift_word$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_drift_nw   <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "drift_stim_catnonword = 0")
t2_bf_drift_nw    <- 1 / t2_hyp_drift_nw$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t2_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_resp_ezdm, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed")
t2_bf_bound  <- 1 / t2_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 3: CSWALD simple + crisk
fe_t3s <- fixef(fit_cswald_simple)
fe_t3c <- fixef(fit_cswald_resp)
t3_rhat_simple <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_simple), na.rm = TRUE)
t3_rhat_crisk  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_cswald_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
t3s_drift_word    <- fmt_est(fe_t3s["drift_stim_catword", ])
t3s_drift_nonword <- fmt_est(fe_t3s["drift_stim_catnonword", ])
t3s_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t3s_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t3s["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t3c_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t3c_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t3c["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
# Tutorial 3: Hypothesis tests
t3_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_cswald_simple, "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword")
t3_bf_drift  <- 1 / t3_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t3_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_cswald_simple, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed")
t3_bf_bound  <- 1 / t3_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 4: DDM
fe_t4a <- fixef(fit_ddm_acc)
fe_t4r <- fixef(fit_ddm_resp)
t4_rhat_acc  <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_acc), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_rhat_resp <- max(brms::rhat(fit_ddm_resp), na.rm = TRUE)
t4_drift_hf  <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqhigh", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_drift_lf  <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqlow", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_drift_vlf <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqvery_low", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_drift_nw  <- round(fe_t4a["drift_freqnonword", "Estimate"], 2)
t4_bound_acc   <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_bound_speed <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["bound_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]))
t4_ndt <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_zr_speed <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionspeed", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_zr_acc   <- fmt_est(plogis(fe_t4r["zr_conditionaccuracy", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)

# Tutorial 4: Hypothesis tests (parallel to Tutorials 1-3)
t4_hyp_bound <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed")
t4_bf_bound  <- 1 / t4_hyp_bound$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio
t4_hyp_drift <- hypothesis(fit_ddm_acc, "drift_freqhigh = drift_freqvery_low")
t4_bf_drift  <- 1 / t4_hyp_drift$hypothesis$Evid.Ratio

# Tutorial 4: EZ-Diffusion (freq) vs full DDM divergences
fe_t4f   <- fixef(fit_acc_ezdm_freq)
t4_ndt_ez  <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4f["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
t4_ndt_ddm <- fmt_est(exp(fe_t4a["ndt_Intercept", c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), 3)
.drift_lvls   <- c("freqhigh", "freqlow", "freqvery_low", "freqnonword")
.drift_ratios <- fe_t4f[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"] /
                 fe_t4a[paste0("drift_", .drift_lvls), "Estimate"]
t4_drift_pct_mean <- round((mean(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_lo   <- round((min(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)
t4_drift_pct_hi   <- round((max(.drift_ratios) - 1) * 100)

# Appendix: Subject-level recovery correlations
extract_subject_params <- function(fit, model_name, n_subjects = 50) {
  co <- coef(fit)$id
  bind_rows(
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "drift_easy",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "drift_conditioneasy"]),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "drift_hard",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "drift_conditionhard"]),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "bound",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = exp(co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "bound_Intercept"])),
    tibble(model = model_name, parameter = "ndt",
           id = 1:n_subjects, recovered = exp(co[1:n_subjects, "Estimate", "ndt_Intercept"]))
  )
}

subject_recovery <- bind_rows(
  extract_subject_params(fit_ezdm_3par, "EZDM 3par"),
  extract_subject_params(fit_cswald_crisk, "CSWALD crisk"),
  extract_subject_params(fit_ddm, "DDM")
)

true_subject <- bind_rows(
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "drift_easy", true_value = drift_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "hard") |> transmute(id, parameter = "drift_hard", true_value = drift_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "bound", true_value = bound_subj),
  true_params_subject |> filter(condition == "easy") |> transmute(id, parameter = "ndt", true_value = ndt_subj)
)

subject_recovery <- subject_recovery |>
  left_join(true_subject, by = c("id", "parameter"))

recovery_cors <- subject_recovery |>
  group_by(model, parameter) |>
  summarise(r = cor(true_value, recovered), .groups = "drop")

recovery_r_min <- round(min(recovery_cors$r), 2)
recovery_r_max <- round(max(recovery_cors$r), 2)
recovery_r_median <- round(median(recovery_cors$r), 2)
```

# Introduction

Consider two participants performing a speeded choice task, for example deciding if a digit is odd or even. Participant A  has an average response time of correct responses of 550 ms and an accuracy of 90%; Participant B has an average response time of correct responses of 600 ms with an accuracy of 95%. Who would you say performed better on the task? An analysis focussing on reaction times would favor A while an analysis focussing on accuracy woudl favor B. However, neither of the summary statistics alone can provide evidence *why* and *how* these participants differ on the level of the underlying cognitive processes. In our exaple, participant A may extract evidence faster but set a more liberal decision threshold, while Participant B may extract evidence at the same rate but set a more cautious threshold that trades speed for accuracy. Traditional analyses focussing on mean RT and accuracy are insufficient for such inferences; they confound effects of different underlying processes and are not process pure measures of the underlying cognitive processes [@frischkorn2026validity].

The by now ubiquotus way to address this issue is to use mathematical models that describe how the underlying latent cognitive processes give rise to the observed behavioral performance. Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) jointly model response times (RTs) and accuracy from speeded decision-making tasks to decompose observed performance into latent cognitive parameters: the rate of evidence accumulation, the amount of evidence required before responding, and the time consumed by non-decisional processes such as stimulus encoding and motor execution. Since their introduction [@ratcliff1978theory], EAMs have become the standard framework for analyzing RT data across perception, memory retrieval, and cognitive control [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @donkin2018response; @evans2019evidence].

The Diffusion Decision Model [DDM; @ratcliff1978theory] is the most widely applied EAM for two-choice tasks. By now it is supported by decades of empirical validation across cognitive domains [@ratcliff2008diffusion]. The DDM is one member of a broader family of accumulation architectures; alternatives include race models such as the Linear Ballistic Accumulator and competitive models in which accumulators inhibit each other [@brown2008lba; @rouder2015lnr; @tillman2020racing; @usher2001lca]. These are beyond the scope of this tutorial, and it will focus only on the DDM [for reviews, see @ratcliff2004comparison; @forstmann2016review; @boag2025expert].

Within the DDM framework, multiple estimation approaches have been proposed that differ in data requirements, computational cost, and their underlying assumptions [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @anders2016shifted; @ratcliff1978theory; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. All of them estimate the same core DDM parameters, drift, boundary separation, non-decision time, and (optionally) relative starting point, but extract these parameters from data at different levels of granularity: from aggregated summary statistics, or from trial-level RT distributions either using distributional approximations or the mathematically accurate DDM or Wiener first-passage time likelihood. Choosing among these approaches involves balancing trade-offs that are complicated by the fact that RT data oftentimes contain contaminant responses, such as fast guesses, or attentional lapses. These bias parameter estimates [@ratcliff2002estimating; @ratcliff2008ez; @boag2025expert] and affect different estimation procedures to varying degrees. Although many software options for estimating DDM parameters have been developed over the recent years, each of the above mentioned approaches required its own specialized software, making cross-approach comparison difficult. The `bmm` R package [@popov2024bmm] now addresses this by implementing three DDM estimation approaches, the EZ-Diffusion Model [`ezdm` in `bmm`; @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion], the Censored-Shifted Wald[`cswald`; @anders2016shifted] as a distributional proxy, and full DDM likelihood estimation [`ddm`]. All three approaches are implemented in a unified Bayesian hierarchical framework built on `brms` [@burkner2017brms] and Stan [@cmdstanr2024]. The consistent interface means that switching between estimation approaches requires changing only the model object, while the formula syntax, prior specification, and post-processing tools remain identical.[^future]

[^future]: The implementation of race-model architectures in `bmm` may follow in future versions of the package.

Estimating DDM parameters within a Bayesian hierarchical framework offers several advantages over the single-subject maximum likelihood approaches that dominated earlier work. Hierarchical estimation borrows data information across participants, producing more stable individual-level estimates even with moderate trial counts [@vandekerckhove2011hierarchical], a common practical constraint in multi-condition designs. Moreover, it provides proper uncertainty quantification through posterior distributions rather than point estimates, and it naturally handles unbalanced cell sizes that arise when some conditions produce few errors [@boehm2018shortcuts]. Furthermore, a unified interface for all three estimation approaches makes cross-approach comparison straightforward: because the formula syntax, prior specification, and post-processing tools are identical, researchers can fit all three approaches and compare their conclusions. As I demonstrate in this tutorial, the Bayesian hierarchical formulation also transforms the EZ-Diffusion Model, originally designed as a quick approximation, into a viable primary analysis tool that produces substantively identical conclusions to the full DDM at a fraction of the computational cost [@chavez2025ez].

This tutorial is written for researchers with basic familiarity with R and hierarchical Bayesian regression models estimated via `brms` who have collected or plan to collect two-choice RT data. After completing the tutorials, you will be able to:

1. Preprocess RT data to detect and handle contaminant responses using `bmm`'s dedicated pre-processing functions.
2. Specify, fit, and evaluate DDM models using the `ezdm`, `cswald`, and `ddm` implementations in `bmm`.
3. Choose among estimation approaches and apply them to empirical data.

The tutorial focuses on the simple (four-parameter) DDM framework for two-choice tasks. It does not cover the full DDM with between-trial variability parameters, race-model architectures (e.g., the LBA or racing diffusion model), multi-alternative choice tasks, or formal model comparison techniques such as leave-one-out cross-validation or bridge sampling; these are available via `brms` but beyond the present scope.

We begin with a data preprocessing section demonstrating how contaminants bias DDM parameter estimates (using simulated data with known ground truth) and introducing `bmm`'s preprocessing tools. We then introduce the empirical dataset used throughout the tutorials, the classic lexical decision study by @wagenmakers2008lexical. Four example use cases then apply the EZ-Diffusion Model, Censored-Shifted Wald, and full DDM to this dataset, each motivated by a limitation of the previous approach, followed by a comparison between the approaches and practical recommendations for their use. The examples are complemented by a short simulated parameter recovery study at both group and individual level provided in the Appendix. Complete R scripts for all examples are available on [OSF]() and [GitHub]() [see also @frischkorn2025tutorial for a companion tutorial on mixture models in `bmm`; @boag2025expert for experimental design guidance].

# Background: Evidence Accumulation Models

## The Diffusion Model Framework

To build intuition for what the DDM captures, consider the following example. In a lexical decision task, a participant sees the letter string "CHAIR" on screen and is instructed to press one of two buttons to indicate if the target stimulus is a "word" or "nonword." Upon stimulus onset, the participant begins extracting evidence such as orthographic regularity, phonological plausibility, or lexical familiarity that accumulates noisily over time toward one of two response boundaries. If the accumulated evidence reaches the "word" boundary first, the participant responds "word"; if it instead reaches the "nonword" boundary, they respond "nonword". The observed RT is the sum of this decision time and non-decisional components such as stimulus encoding and motor execution. See @fig-diffusion-schematic for an illustration of this process.

This example illustrates the core assumptions of the DDM [@ratcliff1978theory; @ratcliff2008diffusion], and it also shows the four parameters that each capture a distinct aspect of the decision process. Each has a mathematical symbol, used in equations and figures, and a name in `bmm`, used in formulas and output; I introduce both here and use them interchangeably throughout the tutorial:

- **Drift Rate** ($\delta$; `drift`): The mean rate of evidence accumulation, reflecting stimulus quality or strength. Higher drift yields faster and more accurate responses.
- **Boundary separation**, or **bound** ($\alpha$; `bound`): The distance between the two response boundaries, capturing *response caution*. Wider boundaries require more evidence, yielding slower but more accurate responses.
- **Non-decision time**, or **ndt** ($\tau$; `ndt`): The portion of the observed RT not attributable to the decision process, encompassing *stimulus encoding* and *motor execution*.
- **Relative starting point** ($\zeta$; `zr`): The starting point of evidence accumulation between the two boundaries, expressed as a proportion relative to the boundary separation (0.5 = unbiased). Values deviating from 0.5 indicate an *a priori response bias* towards the upper or lower response.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diffusion-schematic
#| fig-cap: "Schematic of the Diffusion Decision Model. After stimulus onset, the non-decision time ($\\tau$, shaded region) captures stimulus encoding and motor execution; evidence then accumulates noisily from the starting point ($\\zeta_r$) toward one of two response boundaries separated by distance $\\alpha$, with the mean rate of accumulation given by the drift ($\\delta$). Several example paths are shown (blue: reaching the upper boundary, correct response; red: reaching the lower boundary, error). The distributions attached to each boundary show the resulting response times, right-skewed for correct responses and errors alike (the error distribution's height is exaggerated for visibility)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "03_diffusion_schematic.pdf"))
```

Although these parameters can be used to express the likelihood distribution of response times for responses reaching the upper or lower response boundary, these parameters are not merely mathematical tools or reparametrizations of the observed responses and their response times. From my perspective, using the DDM entails a commitment to assuming that these parameters reflect properties of our cognitive system that are linked to mechanisms that implement them. In addition, they make testable predictions about how experimental manipulations should affect behavior. According to the principle of *selective influence*, manipulations designed to affect a specific cognitive process should primarily change the corresponding model parameter while leaving the others relatively unchanged. For example, stimulus quality manipulations (e.g., degradation, word frequency) should affect drift, whereas *response caution* manipulations (e.g., speed–accuracy instructions) should affect the boundary separation [@voss2004interpreting; @ratcliff2008diffusion]. This selective influence, consistently demonstrated in previous studies, underscores the validity of the DDM with respect to capturing basic properties of the cognitive system [see @boag2025expert, Table 2, for a comprehensive overview].

The four-parameter formulation described above is sometimes called the *simple* or *pure* DDM. The *full* DDM [@ratcliff2002estimating] adds three trial-to-trial variability parameters: variability in drift (trials with unluckily low drift end slowly and often at the wrong boundary, producing slow errors), variability in the starting point (trials starting near the wrong boundary reach it quickly, producing fast errors), and variability in ndt (to account for leading-edge variation in RT distributions). These additions increase the model's flexibility, but also its complexity and computational cost, and the added parameters are often difficult to recover reliably from data [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @boehm2018variability]. For many applications — especially when the goal is to detect condition effects on drift or bound rather than to characterize the precise shape of error RT distributions — the simple DDM is the more parsimonious and statistically powerful choice [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. Moreover, the computational cost of estimating trial-to-trial varibaility parameters in Bayesian hierarchical modeling is high and likely infeasible for larger individual differences studies or experimental designs with several experimental factors.[^feasibility] Therefore, all three estimation approaches in `bmm` are based on the simple DDM framework.

[^feasibility]: In the collaborative estimation exercise reported by @boehm2018variability, a hierarchical data set of 20 simulated participants with a single difficulty manipulation already sat at the edge of what was feasible for expert teams, with one hierarchical fit taking about 14 hours on four cores, another team able to run only a single MCMC chain in the time available, and a third abandoning hierarchical estimation altogether.

## DDM Estimation Approaches in bmm

The `bmm` package implements three approaches for estimating DDM parameters that share the same theoretical framework but differ in data requirements and computational cost. @tbl-model-comparison summarizes the key differences; the distributions named in its Likelihood row are unpacked in the subsections that follow.

| Feature | EZ-Diffusion Model | Censored-Shifted Wald | Full DDM |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `bmm` function | `ezdm()` | `cswald()` | `ddm()` |
| Data level | Aggregated | Trial-level | Trial-level |
| Input | Mean RT, Var RT, accuracy | RT, response | RT, response |
| Parameters | drift ($\delta$), bound ($\alpha$), ndt ($\tau$) (+$\zeta$ in 4par) | drift, bound, ndt (+$\zeta$ in crisk) | drift, bound, ndt (+$\zeta$) |
| Likelihood | Closed-form equations | Shifted Wald | Wiener first-passage time |
| Min trials/cell | ~30 | ~50 | ~50 |
| Starting point ($\zeta$) | 4par only | crisk only | Optional |
| Fitting time | Seconds–minutes | ~4 h (simple), ~18 h (crisk) | ~17–21 hours |
| Best suited for | Exploration, many conditions | Iterative development (simple); response bias at high error rates (crisk) | Confirmatory analysis |

: Summary of the three DDM estimation approaches in `bmm`. Parameter symbols used throughout: drift $\delta$, boundary separation (bound) $\alpha$, non-decision time (ndt) $\tau$, relative starting point $\zeta$. {#tbl-model-comparison}

### EZ-Diffusion Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model [`ezdm` in `bmm`; @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion] was developed to make diffusion model analysis quick and easy by eliminating the need for iterative fitting routines. Its starting point is that for a diffusion process with an unbiased starting point, three quantities — the probability of reaching the upper boundary, the mean decision time, and the variance of the decision time — have closed-form expressions in terms of drift and bound alone. Writing $\delta$ for drift, $\alpha$ for bound, and setting the diffusion noise $s = 1$, with $y = -\alpha\delta$:

$$
P(\text{upper}) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{MDT} = \frac{\alpha}{2\delta} \cdot \frac{1 - e^{y}}{1 + e^{y}}, \qquad
\text{VDT} = \frac{\alpha}{2\delta^{3}} \cdot \frac{2y e^{y} - e^{2y} + 1}{(1 + e^{y})^{2}}
$$

where MDT and VDT are the mean and variance of the decision time, and $n$ below is the number of trials in the cell (`n_trials`). The observed mean RT is MDT plus ndt; the observed RT variance is VDT, since a constant ndt shifts the distribution without spreading it. The original formulation inverted these expressions to compute parameter estimates directly from the observed summary statistics, which is what made EZ-Diffusion analysis a calculator exercise rather than a fitting problem.

`bmm` uses the equations in the forward direction instead, following the probabilistic reformulation of @chavez2025ez. Rather than inverting, it treats the three summary statistics of each cell as noisy observations of their expected values and gives each a sampling distribution:

$$
n_{\text{upper}} \sim \text{Binomial}\big(n, P(\text{upper})\big), \qquad
\overline{\text{RT}} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\tau + \text{MDT},\; \sqrt{\tfrac{\text{VDT}}{n}}\right), \qquad
s^{2}_{\text{RT}} \sim \text{Gamma}\!\left(\tfrac{n-1}{2},\; \tfrac{n-1}{2\,\text{VDT}}\right)
$$

Casting the model this way is what makes hierarchical estimation with arbitrary regression structures on the parameters possible: there is now a likelihood to which priors, random effects, and predictors can be attached. It also makes the dependence on preprocessing explicit. The data entering this likelihood are $n_{\text{upper}}$, $\overline{\text{RT}}$, and $s^{2}_{\text{RT}}$ — nothing else — so anything that distorts those three numbers distorts the parameter estimates directly. This is why the preprocessing section that follows is not housekeeping.

The speed comes at the cost of two assumptions: no trial-to-trial variability in any parameter, and an unbiased starting point ($\zeta = 0.5$). When these are violated, estimates can be biased; drift, for example, is attenuated at high values when the generating process has trial-to-trial variability. But the model remains a surprisingly powerful tool for detecting condition effects, with prior simulation work reporting statistical power comparable to or higher than the full DDM [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @ratcliff2008ez; @wagenmakers2008extensions]; we return to this claim in the Discussion.

Two extensions matter here. *Robust-EZ* fits a two-component mixture — a uniform distribution for contaminant RTs and an ex-Gaussian for the decision process — and feeds the ex-Gaussian component's mean and variance, rather than the raw sample moments, into the EZ equations [@wagenmakers2008extensions]; this is the mixture method of `ezdm_summary_stats()` introduced in the Data Preprocessing section. A four-parameter extension estimates the relative starting point from boundary-specific RT moments — the mean and variance computed separately for upper- and lower-boundary responses [@grasman2009ez; @srivastava2016moments]; we use it in Tutorial 2.

### Censored-Shifted Wald Model

The EZ-Diffusion Model's speed comes from working with summary statistics, but this means it cannot incorporate trial-level predictors or preserve information about the shape of the RT distribution. The full DDM preserves all of this but is computationally expensive. The Censored-Shifted Wald [`cswald` in `bmm`; @anders2016shifted] offers a middle path: it models individual RTs directly, preserving distributional information and enabling trial-level predictors, while remaining substantially faster than the full DDM.

The Censored-Shifted Wald achieves this by using the shifted Wald (inverse Gaussian) distribution. The shifted Wald describes the *first-passage time* — the moment an accumulation path like those in @fig-diffusion-schematic first touches a boundary — for a diffusion process with a single *absorbing* boundary, meaning a boundary at which the process stops as soon as it arrives [@anders2016shifted]. This is a simpler process than the two-boundary framework of the DDM, and therefore faster to evaluate. Crucially, when error rates are low — because drift is high, bound is wide, or responses are biased toward the correct boundary — the shifted Wald parameters closely approximate those of the distribution that underlies the full DDM. That distribution is the *Wiener first-passage time distribution*, or *Wiener distribution* for short: the two-boundary counterpart of the shifted Wald, giving the joint distribution of the time taken and the boundary reached. We describe it in the next subsection but two [@miller2018shifted]. In other words, when most responses are correct, the decision process behaves as if there were effectively only one boundary to reach, and the Censored-Shifted Wald captures this well.

Two versions implemented in `bmm` handle error responses differently, and both borrow their logic from the statistics of waiting times.

The *simple* version treats an error as a *censored* correct response. The idea is this: the model describes how long it takes to reach the correct boundary, but on an error trial the correct boundary was never reached. What the trial tells us is not a completion time but a lower bound — whatever the correct-boundary process would eventually have taken, it was longer than the RT we observed, because at that moment the participant had responded and we stopped observing.

This translates directly into the likelihood. A correct response at time $t$ contributes the shifted Wald density $f$, while an error at time $t$ contributes the *survival function* $S(t) = 1 - F(t)$, where $F$ is the cumulative distribution function of $f$. The survival function is simply the probability that the correct-boundary process had not finished by $t$:

$$
\mathcal{L}(t) =
\begin{cases}
f(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) & \text{correct response} \\[4pt]
S(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) = 1 - \displaystyle\int_{\tau}^{t} f(u \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau)\, du & \text{error}
\end{cases}
$$

with the shifted Wald density itself given by

$$
f(t \mid \delta, \alpha, \tau) = \frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{2\pi (t - \tau)^{3}}} \, \exp\!\left(-\frac{\big(\alpha - \delta (t-\tau)\big)^{2}}{2 (t - \tau)}\right), \qquad t > \tau
$$

again with $s = 1$. Two consequences follow, and they are the reason this version works at all. First, error trials are *used*, not discarded — they enter the likelihood, just through a different function. They also remain genuinely informative: a fast error tells the model that the correct-boundary process was still unfinished very early, which is evidence against a high-drift, wide-bound parameterization, so errors constrain drift and bound even though the model never predicts which boundary was reached. Second, a censored trial cannot pin down a completion time, only bound it from below, so it constrains the parameters less tightly than a correct response does.

That second point is where the version's limits come from. As the proportion of censored trials grows, more of the data constrains the parameters only loosely, and the approximation degrades — hence the guideline of roughly 20% errors [@miller2018shifted]. Note that this converges with the argument made above from the other direction: high error rates are also exactly the regime in which the one-boundary picture stops approximating the two-boundary process well. Both routes lead to the same restriction, which is why a single guideline covers them.

The *competing-risks* (crisk) version takes the other route. Rather than censoring errors, it models both correct and error RTs explicitly, as two independent racing shifted Wald processes that share a non-decision time; the first to finish produces the observed response. This also makes it possible to estimate the relative starting point. At higher error rates, or when response bias is the question, the competing-risks version provides a better approximation to the Wiener distribution [@miller2018shifted].

### Full DDM Likelihood Estimation

The full DDM estimation approach [`ddm` in `bmm`] uses the Wiener first-passage time distribution, which jointly models both the RT and the response boundary that was reached [@ratcliff1978theory; @vandekerckhove2007fitting]. Unlike the Censored-Shifted Wald, which approximates the decision process with one or two independent single-boundary accumulators, the full DDM models the two-boundary process directly. This means it simultaneously captures the probability of reaching each boundary *and* the complete distribution of times to reach it, making it the mathematically most accurate and complete characterization of the evidence accumulation process within a single likelihood function. However, evaluating the Wiener distribution's density involves an infinite series that must be truncated adaptively, making likelihood computation substantially more expensive than for the `ezdm` or `cswald` approaches [@navarro2009fast]. Various estimation methods have been developed over the years, including chi-square fitting [@ratcliff2002estimating], maximum likelihood [@vandekerckhove2007fitting; @voss2007fastdm], and hierarchical Bayesian methods [@vandekerckhove2011hierarchical; @wiecki2013hddm]. In `bmm`, the full DDM is fitted via Stan's `wiener_lpdf()` function, which implements efficient series truncation within a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework.

## Estimating DDM Parameters with Existing Software

Each of these approaches has established software, and most packages have historically served a single approach: `fast-dm` for $\chi^2$ and maximum-likelihood fitting of the full DDM [@voss2007fastdm], HDDM for hierarchical Bayesian DDM estimation in Python [@wiecki2013hddm], `rtdists` for DDM and LBA densities in R [@singmann2016rtdists], and spreadsheet or script implementations of the original EZ-Diffusion equations [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion]. The exception is `EMC2` [@stevenson2026emc2], which, like `bmm`, sets out to provide a general hierarchical Bayesian framework for evidence accumulation models, and which is therefore the closest point of comparison. @tbl-software summarizes how these packages relate to `bmm`.

| Feature | Per-subject ML (`fast-dm`, `rtdists`) | Standalone EZ-Diffusion | HDDM | `EMC2` | `bmm` |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Estimation | Maximum likelihood or $\chi^2$ | Closed-form calculation | Hierarchical Bayesian | Hierarchical Bayesian | Hierarchical Bayesian |
| Sampler | Numerical optimization | None | Slice sampling (PyMC) | Particle Metropolis-within-Gibbs | Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Stan) |
| Uncertainty | Point estimates (+ bootstrap) | Point estimates | Posterior distributions | Posterior distributions | Posterior distributions |
| Multiple conditions | Fit separately per condition | Computed separately per cell | Regression syntax | Formula per parameter (`design()`) | Formula per parameter (`bmf()`) |
| Inference over conditions | Stepwise: test point estimates, ignoring uncertainty [@boehm2018shortcuts] | Stepwise | One step | One step | One step |
| Continuous predictors | No | No | Limited | Yes | Yes |
| Different predictors per parameter | No | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Grouping factors | Not applicable | Not applicable | Participants | Participants | Any `brms` structure (participants, items, crossed) |
| Parameter covariance across participants | No | No | No | Full, blocked, diagonal, or factor-analytic | Optional, via linked terms |
| Trials required per cell | Several hundred | ~30 | ~50 | ~50 | ~30 (`ezdm`) to ~50 (trial-level) |
| Models covered | Full DDM | EZ-Diffusion | Full DDM | Full DDM, LBA, RDM, LNR, custom likelihoods | Three DDM approaches, one interface |
| Post-processing | Package-specific | Manual | Package-specific | Package-specific | The `brms` ecosystem |

: Comparison of `bmm` with existing software for estimating DDM parameters. {#tbl-software}

The differences between `bmm` and `EMC2` run in both directions, and it is worth being explicit about which is which. `EMC2` covers far more of the evidence accumulation family. It implements the full DDM including the across-trial variability parameters, the linear ballistic accumulator, the racing diffusion model, the lognormal race model, and signal detection models; it accepts user-supplied likelihood functions, so a model it does not ship can still be fitted within its machinery; and it extends to joint models of behavior and fMRI time series. It also treats the group level as a modeling target in its own right, estimating a full covariance matrix across participants' parameters by default, with diagonal, blocked, and factor-analytic alternatives, and it provides marginal likelihoods via bridge sampling for formal model comparison. The DDM is currently the only evidence accumulation model in `bmm`, and only in its simple form. If the question concerns a race architecture, the across-trial variability parameters, or the covariance structure of parameters across people, `EMC2` is the better tool.

What `bmm` offers instead is the `brms` interface and everything downstream of it. Both packages specify designs through R formulas, one per model parameter, so the difference is not regression syntax as such; it is that in `bmm` those are `brms` formulas. The random-effects syntax, the prior syntax, and the whole post-processing ecosystem are the ones you already use for mixed models. That also brings `brms`'s full range of random-effects structures. `EMC2` places participants under a group-level distribution, whereas in `bmm` any grouping factor in the data is available, so the lexical decision data analyzed below could carry by-word random effects alongside by-participant ones, which for item-based paradigms is often the more defensible specification. `bmm` is also the only package that offers the EZ-Diffusion and Censored-Shifted Wald approaches alongside the full DDM behind one interface, which is what makes the staged workflow of this tutorial possible: you can move between the three without rewriting your analysis. Finally, the DDM is one model family among several in `bmm`, which also implements measurement models for visual working memory and for working memory capacity [@frischkorn2025tutorial; @frischkorn2026m3], so a research program that spans paradigms can keep one specification and post-processing workflow across all of them.

The two packages also sample differently, and here neither dominates. `EMC2` uses particle Metropolis-within-Gibbs [@gunawan2020pmwg]: a Gibbs step updates the group-level mean and covariance matrix, and each participant's parameters are then updated by a particle-Metropolis step whose proposals are drawn from that estimated covariance. This is the algorithm's motivating property. DDM parameters trade off against one another, drift against bound and bound against ndt, so a participant's posterior has pronounced ridges, and proposing along the estimated covariance moves along such a ridge rather than across it. The algorithm also requires only that the likelihood can be *evaluated*, not differentiated, which is what makes the LBA and the across-trial variability parameters tractable. `bmm` inherits Stan's No-U-Turn Sampler, which uses the gradient of the log posterior to follow the same ridges and which reports divergent transitions when the geometry defeats it, a diagnostic that Metropolis-based samplers do not provide. The price is that Stan needs a differentiable log density, which is one reason the `ddm` approach in `bmm` implements the simple DDM. The two samplers trade gradient information against generality of the likelihood, and which trade is better depends on the model you want to fit rather than on the package.

## The `bmm` Workflow

Fitting any of the three approaches with `bmm` follows the same three steps, and those steps are identical for every measurement model in the package:

1. **Define the model.** A constructor function — `ezdm()`, `cswald()`, or `ddm()` — returns a model object carrying everything `bmm` needs to build the likelihood: which columns of your data hold the response variables, and which version of the model you want.
2. **Specify predictor formulas.** The `bmmformula()` function, or its shorthand `bmf()`, defines how experimental conditions and individual differences predict each model parameter. The syntax is the `brms` formula syntax [@burkner2017brms], including random effects.
3. **Fit the model.** Pass the model object, the formula, and the data to `bmm()`, which translates the specification into a `brms` model and hands it to Stan for estimation.

You supply two things: how the relevant variables are labeled in your data, and which parameters should vary over which conditions. `bmm` supplies the rest — it assembles the likelihood, fixes the parameters a given version does not estimate, sets the link functions, chooses weakly informative default priors, and runs consistency checks on the data before fitting. The relationship between `bmm` and `brms` is the same as that between `brms` and Stan: each layer removes boilerplate from the one below without hiding it, and you can inspect what was generated at any point (`fit$formula`, `fit$family`, `fit$data`).

Because `bmm` builds on `brms`, fitted models inherit the `brms` post-processing ecosystem: `summary()` for convergence diagnostics, `pp_check()` for posterior predictive checks, `fixef()` and `ranef()` for parameter estimates, and `hypothesis()` for Bayes Factors. Every tutorial below re-runs these same three steps with a different model object.

## Contaminant Processes in RT Data

Not all observed RTs arise from the evidence accumulation process that EAMs are designed to characterize. *Fast guesses*, responses emitted before meaningful stimulus evaluation, produce RTs below what any accumulation-to-bound process could generate, with accuracy near chance. *Slow outliers* result from attentional lapses or distraction, producing abnormally long RTs that inflate RT variance. Both violate the core assumption that each observed RT reflects a decision time plus non-decision time [@ratcliff1993methods; @ratcliff2002estimating]. Even moderate contamination rates (3–5%) can substantially bias EAM parameter estimates [@ratcliff2008ez; @wagenmakers2008extensions], and fixed cutoffs bias the summary statistics themselves [@ulrich1994effects]. The next section demonstrates the magnitude of this problem using simulation and introduces `bmm`'s tools for addressing it.

# Data Preprocessing: Principles and Tools

Data preprocessing is not merely a housekeeping step; it is a substantive methodological decision that directly affects parameter estimates. A common approach is to apply hard RT cutoffs — removing all RTs below 200 ms or above 3,000 ms, say — but such cutoffs are arbitrary and can themselves introduce bias by removing legitimate fast or slow responses. The `bmm` package provides a principled, model-based alternative: a mixture-model approach that separates contaminant responses from the core decision process probabilistically.

This section shows what contaminants do to EAM parameters and introduces the two functions you will use in every subsequent tutorial. The simulation evidence behind the recommendations is reported in Appendix A.

## Demonstrating Contaminant Bias

To illustrate the severity of contaminant bias under controlled conditions, we use simulated data generated from a DDM with known parameters (drift: 2.5 for an easy, 1.0 for a hard condition; bound: 1.5; ndt: 0.3) for 50 participants, each completing 200 trials per condition. We then replace 3% of the trials with each of three contaminant processes — *fast guesses* (uniform RTs between 100 ms and the participant's ndt, responses at chance), *delayed start-ups* (a uniform delay of up to 2 s added to the RT the decision process produced), and *informationless responses* (the trial redrawn from the same DDM with drift set to zero) — to produce a contaminated version of the same dataset. These are the processes evaluated in the Monte Carlo study of Appendix A; they differ in a way that turns out to matter more than their rate, namely in whether the contaminants they produce can be told apart from ordinary decisions at all.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rt-density
#| fig-cap: "Where the three contaminant processes place their trials, relative to the RT distribution the decision process produces. Each panel shows the core distribution (grey) and the injected contaminants (orange); both are scaled to the same area, so the panels compare the location of the two components rather than their relative frequency (contaminants are 3% of trials per process). Fast guesses fall entirely below the core, delayed start-ups partly overlap it, and informationless responses overlap it almost completely."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "10_rt_density.pdf"))
```

@fig-rt-density shows where each process puts its contaminants. Fast guesses form a spike below the fastest RT the decision process can produce, so they are separable by inspection; delayed start-ups spread across and beyond the slow tail; and informationless responses sit almost on top of the core distribution, particularly in the hard condition, where they are indistinguishable from ordinary decisions by RT alone. @fig-sumstats-bias shows the downstream impact: contaminated data produce inflated RT variance, shifted mean RT, and reduced accuracy. Because EZ-Diffusion parameters are direct transformations of these summary statistics, any distortion propagates directly to biased parameter estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sumstats-bias
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of summary statistics (mean RT, variance of RT, accuracy) computed from contaminated versus clean data. Each box spans the interquartile range across 50 simulated participants. Contaminant responses inflate RT variance, shift mean RT, and reduce accuracy."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "10_sumstats_bias.pdf"))
```

## Identifying Contaminant Responses with `flag_contaminant_rts()`

The `flag_contaminant_rts()` function implements a mixture-model approach: within each participant × condition cell, an expectation–maximization (EM) algorithm, an iterative procedure that alternates between classifying trials and re-estimating the distribution parameters, decomposes the RT distribution into a core component and a uniform contaminant component, returning the posterior probability that each trial is a contaminant. The core component can be ex-Gaussian, lognormal, or inverse Gaussian; all three are right-skewed families commonly used to describe RT distributions, and they differ mainly in how heavy a right tail they allow. The ex-Gaussian is the default because it is the only one of the three that reproduces the mean and variance of diffusion-model RTs without bias; the lognormal and inverse-Gaussian cores misfit the diffusion tail and are biased even on clean data (Appendix A). Pass `maxit = 500`: with the default cap of 100 iterations the EM stops early in a few percent of cells and the function then returns `NA` probabilities, which a subsequent `filter()` would silently drop along with the whole cell.

```{r}
#| label: flag-contaminant
data_flagged <- data_contaminated |>
  group_by(id, condition) |>
  mutate(
    contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(
      rt,
      distribution = "exgaussian",
      contaminant_bound = c("min", "max"),
      maxit = 500
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

The `contaminant_bound` argument specifies at which ends of the RT distribution contaminants are expected, here both fast guesses (`"min"`) and slow outliers (`"max"`). Trials with `contam_prob > 0.5` are classified as likely contaminants. The 0.5 threshold is a natural decision boundary: above it, a trial is more likely a contaminant than a legitimate response under the mixture model. On the simulated dataset introduced above, the trials it flags are almost always genuine contaminants (91% of them, against 0.3% of clean trials falsely flagged), but it finds only 29% of the contaminants that are there, and how many it finds depends entirely on the process: 46% of the fast guesses, 33% of the delayed start-ups, and 7% of the informationless responses, which no rule based on RT alone can separate from ordinary decisions. This is worth taking seriously before using the probabilities to exclude trials: what the mixture model reliably tells you is that a flagged trial is suspect, not that an unflagged one is clean. For computing summary statistics the picture is better than these detection rates suggest, because down-weighting does not require confident classification of individual trials — on the same data the mixture method still cuts the error in mean RT and RT variance by a factor of about four to nine in the easy condition and about two in the hard one, relative to no contaminant handling. The companion script `scripts/10b_preprocessing_comparison.R` quantifies classification performance (sensitivity, specificity, and F1 scores, the harmonic mean of precision and recall) across candidate core distributions and contaminant-bound settings.^[`validate_fast_guesses()` provides a principled check that flagged fast trials actually show random guessing behavior by computing a Bayes Factor (introduced in Tutorial 1) for H0: accuracy = 0.5 among flagged trials.]

When using contaminant probabilities to exclude trials before trial-level model fitting (`cswald`, `ddm`), two approaches are available. *Threshold-based flagging* excludes all trials above a fixed cutoff (typically `contam_prob > 0.5`). This is deterministic and straightforward, but treats a trial with `contam_prob = 0.51` identically to one with `contam_prob = 0.99`. *Probabilistic flagging* instead draws a Bernoulli variable for each trial using the contaminant probability as the exclusion rate: `rbinom(n, 1, contam_prob)`. Trials with high contaminant probability are very likely excluded, while borderline trials have a proportional chance of retention, better reflecting the uncertainty in the classification. The companion script compares both approaches; in practice, they yield similar results for well-separated contaminant distributions, but probabilistic flagging is more principled when contaminant probabilities cluster near the decision boundary. For `ezdm` fitting, neither approach is needed; the mixture method in `ezdm_summary_stats()` handles contaminants directly through down-weighting.

## Computing Summary Statistics with `ezdm_summary_stats()`

For `ezdm` fitting, raw trial-level data must be aggregated into summary statistics. The `ezdm_summary_stats()` function provides three aggregation methods: `simple` (standard mean and variance), `robust` (the median together with a variance derived from the interquartile range, $(\mathrm{IQR}/1.349)^2$ — 1.349 is the IQR of a standard normal distribution, so the ratio estimates the SD — with a MAD-based alternative available via the `robust_scale` argument), and `mixture` (a uniform-plus-core mixture fitted by expectation–maximization that returns the mean and variance of the fitted core distribution — the robust-EZ estimator of @wagenmakers2008extensions). The robust estimators are the ones @chavez2026robust proposed for the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model. The mixture method integrates contaminant detection and summary statistic computation into a single step; note that what @chavez2026robust call the "robust EZ-DDM" is the median/IQR method, whereas Wagenmakers et al.'s "robust-EZ" is the mixture method — two different estimators under similar names.

```{r}
#| label: ezdm-sumstats
data_sumstats <- data_contaminated |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(
      rt, response,
      version  = "3par",
      method   = "mixture",
      distribution = "exgaussian",
      maxit    = 500
    ),
    .by = c(id, condition)
  )
```

This produces one row per participant per condition. The `mixture` method handles contaminant detection and aggregation in a single step: rather than first excluding outliers and then computing statistics, it simultaneously estimates the core distribution's mean and variance while down-weighting contaminant contributions.

The result is the data format `ezdm()` expects, and it is worth looking at directly, because the difference between the summary-statistic and trial-level approaches is a difference in what the data frame contains. Here are the first rows of the aggregated lexical decision data we build in the next section:

```{r}
#| label: show-ezdm-data
#| eval: true
head(data_acc_ezdm)
```

Each row is one participant × condition × stimulus category cell. `mean_rt` and `var_rt` are the moments of the RT distribution in that cell, `n_upper` counts responses at the upper boundary, and `n_trials` gives the cell size; `contaminant_prop` records what proportion of the cell the mixture model down-weighted. Those four columns — mean, variance, upper count, total count — are the entire input to the EZ-Diffusion Model. Everything the raw trials contained beyond them is discarded, which is both why the approach is fast and why it cannot take trial-level predictors.

The trial-level approaches of Tutorials 3 and 4 take the data in its original long format instead, one row per trial:

```{r}
#| label: show-triallevel-data
#| eval: true
head(data_accuracy_clean)
```

Here `rt` holds the response time in **seconds** and `response` holds the boundary reached, coded `"upper"` or `"lower"`. Those two columns are what `cswald()` and `ddm()` need; the remaining columns are available as predictors. Note the unit: `bmm` does not inspect or convert your RT scale, so if your data are in milliseconds you must divide by 1000 before fitting, or the ndt estimates and their priors will be badly mismatched.

## Which Method to Use

Use the **mixture method** with the ex-Gaussian distribution as your default for `ezdm` preprocessing. In the Monte Carlo study reported in Appendix A it is the only method that recovers drift, bound, and ndt without bias when the data are clean, and it removes most of the damage done by delayed start-ups and by fast guesses that fall outside the core RT distribution. It cannot see contaminants that overlap the core — informationless responses, trials answered without stimulus information at ordinary speed and with chance accuracy — and no summary-statistic method corrects the loss of accuracy such trials cause, which is where the experimental safeguards of @boag2025expert (instructions, feedback on too-fast and too-slow responses, breaks) do the work that preprocessing cannot. Pass `maxit = 500`; with the default cap of 100 iterations the EM stops early in a few percent of cells and `ezdm_summary_stats()` silently substitutes the robust statistics.

Use the **robust method** when the mixture model's EM algorithm cannot converge, which happens in cells with very few trials (we hit exactly this case in Tutorial 2). @chavez2026robust make a broader case for it: across a large simulation study they show that replacing the moments with the median and the IQR-based variance leaves hypothesis tests on drift effects as accurate as the standard summary statistics on clean data, and preserves that accuracy under contamination, where the standard moments lose it. The trade-off concerns absolute parameter values rather than condition effects. On right-skewed RT distributions the median falls below the mean and the IQR-based variance below the variance, and once the EZ equations turn these statistics into parameters the shortfall lands in drift and bound rather than in ndt: at the parameter values of our simulations drift comes out roughly 10% too high and bound roughly 10% too low, while ndt is nearly unaffected, because the smaller variance also shortens the implied decision time by about as much as the median falls short of the mean (Appendix A). These biases are close to multiplicative and the same in every cell, so condition contrasts are inflated by the same proportion (drift values that are both 10% too high differ by 10% too much) and correlations between individuals are untouched.

With either method, hard RT cutoffs are unnecessary: in Appendix A a 150 ms/5 s pre-filter changed nothing under two of the three contaminant processes and reduced the damage of fast guesses only modestly, and fixed cutoffs truncate legitimate responses once they approach the leading edge of the RT distribution [@ulrich1994effects]. Appendix A also validates the mixture method against the hard cutoffs used in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis. All subsequent tutorials use the mixture method, with the robust method applied where cell sizes are too small for EM convergence.

# The Lexical Decision Dataset

With the preprocessing toolkit established, we now turn to the empirical dataset that serves as the running example for all tutorials. We use the classic lexical decision study by @wagenmakers2008lexical, available as `speed_acc` in the `rtdists` R package [@singmann2016rtdists]. This dataset is ideal for a tutorial for several reasons: it is publicly available and widely used as a benchmark in the diffusion modeling literature, its experimental design has clear and well-tested EAM predictions, and published parameter estimates from the original analysis provide reference values for validating our results.

In this experiment, 17 participants classified letter strings as words or nonwords under two instruction conditions: *speed emphasis* (respond as quickly as possible) and *accuracy emphasis* (respond as accurately as possible). Stimuli included words of varying frequency (high, low, very low) and matched nonwords, creating a 2 (emphasis) × 2 (stimulus category) within-subjects design with approximately 460 trials per cell per participant.

This design maps cleanly onto the selective influence principle introduced in the Background: emphasis should primarily affect bound, and stimulus category should primarily affect drift.

## Data Preparation

We load the data, convert factors to character (needed because `response` and `stim_cat` have different factor level sets), and remove 6 recording failures and all trials flagged as `censor`, which are the trials the original study excluded. Note that the raw `response` column codes those recording failures with the level `"error"`: in `speed_acc` this means *no valid response was recorded*, not an incorrect response. Incorrect responses are identified later, by comparing `response` against `stim_cat`.^[The `censor` flag in the raw dataset is unrelated to the statistical *censoring* of error RTs used by the Censored-Shifted Wald in Tutorial 3. The companion script `scripts/01_prepare_lexical_data.R` contains the full data preparation code for this section.]

```{r}
#| label: data-load
data("speed_acc", package = "rtdists")

data_lexical <- speed_acc |>
  mutate(
    response = as.character(response),
    stim_cat = as.character(stim_cat),
    condition = factor(condition, levels = c("speed", "accuracy"))
  ) |>
  filter(response != "error", censor == FALSE)
```

For EAMs, the response variable must be binary, indicating which of the two decision boundaries was reached. Two codings are possible, each answering a different question:

- **Accuracy-coded** (upper = correct, lower = error): Drift reflects how quickly evidence for the *correct answer* accumulates. This is the standard approach for testing selective influence.
- **Response-coded** (upper = "word" response, lower = "nonword" response): Drift reflects evidence toward saying *"word"* specifically, positive for word stimuli, negative or near zero for nonwords. The relative starting point ($\zeta$) captures response bias toward saying "word."

```{r}
#| label: data-recode
# Accuracy-coded: correct = upper, error = lower
data_accuracy <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == stim_cat, "upper", "lower"))

# Response-coded: "word" response = upper, "nonword" response = lower
data_response <- data_lexical |>
  mutate(response = ifelse(response == "word", "upper", "lower"))
```

We apply contaminant detection and compute summary statistics for the EZ-Diffusion tutorials.

```{r}
#| label: data-preprocess
# Flag contaminant trials
data_accuracy <- data_accuracy |>
  group_by(id, condition, stim_cat) |>
  mutate(
    contam_prob = flag_contaminant_rts(
      rt, distribution = "exgaussian",
      contaminant_bound = c("min", "max")
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

# Clean trial-level data (for the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM)
data_accuracy_clean <- data_accuracy |> filter(contam_prob <= 0.5)
data_response_clean <- data_response |>
  semi_join(data_accuracy_clean, by = c("id", "condition", "stim_cat", "rt"))

# EZ-Diffusion summary statistics (3par, accuracy-coded). The response-coded 4par
# statistics use version = "4par" with method = "robust", because sparse
# minority-boundary cells break the mixture method's EM step (see script)
data_acc_ezdm <- data_accuracy |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "3par",
                       method = "mixture", distribution = "exgaussian"),
    .by = c(id, condition, stim_cat)
  )
```

The `semi_join()` deserves a brief explanation: it keeps exactly those response-coded trials whose accuracy-coded counterpart survived contaminant exclusion. Because both data frames contain the same trials, only coded differently, the combination of participant, condition, stimulus category, and RT identifies each trial and works as a matching key.

# Tutorial 1: Exploring Condition Effects with the EZ-Diffusion Model

Let's start with the simplest and fastest DDM estimation approach in `bmm`: the EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm`). Because it fits in seconds rather than hours, it is the natural first step for exploring condition effects. The central question is: *Do speed–accuracy emphasis and stimulus category selectively influence different cognitive parameters?*^[The companion script `scripts/11_tutorial1_ezdm_3par.R` contains the full executable code for this tutorial.]

## Model Specification

Specifying an EAM in `bmm` involves two objects: a model object that defines the measurement model and maps data columns to model components, and a formula object that specifies the predictor structure for each parameter. The `ezdm()` function creates the model object:

```{r}
#| label: t1-model
#| eval: true
model_acc <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = "mean_rt",
  var_rt   = "var_rt",
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "3par"
)
```

The formula is specified using `bmf()`, which allows separate regression formulas for each parameter. We include stimulus category as a predictor on drift (to test for evidence quality differences) and emphasis condition as a predictor on bound (to test for response caution differences). Random slopes allow each participant's parameters to vary by condition: `(0 + stim_cat | id)` estimates participant-specific drift for words and nonwords, while `(0 + condition | id)` estimates participant-specific boundary settings under speed and accuracy emphasis. The `0 +` in these formulas suppresses the intercept, so the model estimates one coefficient per factor level, separate drifts for words and nonwords, separate bounds for speed and accuracy emphasis, rather than an intercept plus a difference. This makes the `fixef()` output below directly interpretable.

Each parameter uses a *link function* that determines how the linear predictor maps onto the parameter scale. Drift can take any real value, positive when evidence favors the upper boundary, negative when it favors the lower boundary, so it uses an *identity link*, meaning the regression coefficients are directly on the drift scale. Boundary separation and non-decision time, by contrast, must be strictly positive (a negative boundary or negative encoding time is meaningless), so they use a *log link*: the regression coefficients are on the log scale and must be exponentiated to obtain the parameter estimate. This is analogous to using a log link in Poisson regression to ensure predicted counts are positive. In practice, this means that when interpreting `fixef()` output, drift coefficients can be read directly, while bound and ndt coefficients require exponentiation (we demonstrate this below).

```{r}
#| label: t1-formula
#| eval: true
formula_acc <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

We use `bmm`'s default priors throughout Tutorial 1. Before accepting any set of defaults it is worth seeing what they are, which `default_prior()` will tell you for any combination of formula, data, and model:

```{r}
#| label: t1-default-prior
#| eval: true
default_prior(formula_acc, data_acc_ezdm, model_acc)
```

The `dpar` column identifies which model parameter each prior applies to, and `class` distinguishes population-level coefficients (`b`) from random-effect standard deviations (`sd`) and their correlations (`cor`). Note that the priors on `bound` and `ndt` are stated on the log scale, matching their link functions, so a `normal(0, 0.5)` prior on `bound` is a prior over roughly 0.4 to 2.7 on the natural scale rather than over −1 to 1. Override any of them with `brms::prior()` (see Practical Guidelines).

If you do specify custom priors, verify that they produce plausible data before you look at your own: `bmm(..., sample_prior = "only")` samples from the prior alone, and `pp_check()` on the result shows you what RT distributions your priors imply. We skip that step here because the defaults are calibrated for typical RT data, but it is not optional once you depart from them.

## Model Fitting

Fit the model with `bmm()`, which wraps `brms::brm()` with the model-specific likelihood. Setting `sample_prior = "yes"` stores prior samples, which the Savage-Dickey tests below require; `file` caches the fitted model to disk, so re-running the script does not re-fit it. The `control` arguments tune Stan's sampler: `adapt_delta` sets how cautiously the sampler takes steps (higher values mean smaller, safer steps) and `max_treedepth` caps how far a single step can travel. The values below are safe defaults for EAMs, and every subsequent tutorial reuses them.

```{r}
#| label: t1-fit
fit_acc_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_acc,
  data    = data_acc_ezdm,
  model   = model_acc,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_acc")
)
```

Fitting completed in approximately 30 seconds with 5 parallel chains. Convergence should always be verified before interpreting results. The two key diagnostics are $\hat{R}$ (which should be below 1.01 for all parameters) and effective sample size (ESS, which should be at least 400 for reliable posterior summaries). Both can be inspected via `summary(fit_acc_ezdm)`, which displays these diagnostics for every parameter. For this model, the maximum $\hat{R}$ was `r round(t1_rhat, 3)` and the minimum bulk ESS was `r round(t1_ess)`, indicating that the chains mixed well and the posterior was adequately sampled.^[If convergence issues arise, standard remedies include increasing the number of iterations, raising `adapt_delta` (e.g., to 0.95 or 0.99), or simplifying the random-effects structure. See the Troubleshooting section in Practical Guidelines for details.]

## Model Evaluation

Before interpreting parameter estimates, we verify model fit via a posterior predictive check (@fig-t1-ppcheck), which overlays response-time distributions simulated from the posterior on the observed distributions; close overlap across both the bulk and the tails indicates that the model reproduces the data it was fit to. One caveat is specific to the EZ-Diffusion Model: because it is fit to three summary statistics per cell rather than to individual RTs, its posterior predictive check can only confirm that those moments, mean RT, RT variance, and accuracy, are recovered, and cannot detect misfit in the finer shape of the RT distribution. The trial-level Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, which model individual RTs (including the separate distributions of correct and error responses), yield more diagnostic checks; we return to these in Tutorials 3 and 4.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the EZ-Diffusion 3-parameter model fitted to the Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data. Close overlap between observed (dark) and predicted (light) distributions indicates adequate model fit."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_pp_check.pdf"))
```

Extract the population-level estimates with `fixef()`:

```{r}
#| label: t1-params
#| eval: true
fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)
```

Read this table one link function at a time. The two `drift_` rows use the identity link, so the `Estimate` column is already on the drift scale and can be read off directly. The `bound_` and `ndt_` rows use the log link, so their estimates are on the log scale and mean nothing until you exponentiate them. `Q2.5` and `Q97.5` bound the 95% credible interval, and they transform the same way — exponentiate the interval limits rather than trying to build an interval around the exponentiated mean.

```{r}
#| label: t1-params-transform
#| eval: true
exp(fixef(fit_acc_ezdm)[c("bound_conditionspeed", "bound_conditionaccuracy"), ])
```

This is the step you will repeat for every log-link parameter in every model below, so it is worth doing explicitly once rather than reaching for a helper.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t1-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion parameter estimates from the accuracy-coded analysis. Left: drift by stimulus category. Right: bound by emphasis condition. Points show posterior means; error bars show 95% credible intervals."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "11_param_estimates.pdf"))
```

The emphasis manipulation shows the expected effect on bound (@fig-t1-params): speed emphasis produced lower bound ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_speed`) than accuracy emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t1_bound_acc`), reflecting reduced response caution. Drift estimates are nominally higher for word stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_word`) than nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t1_drift_nonword`), but the difference is small; collapsing all words into a single category averages across high-, low-, and very-low-frequency items that differ strongly in drift, as Tutorial 4 shows. Non-decision time was estimated at $\tau$ = `r t1_ndt` seconds. The bound result already demonstrates the core value of EAMs: a traditional analysis comparing mean RTs could not distinguish whether speed-emphasis participants were faster because they processed evidence more efficiently or because they required less evidence. We return to drift effects in Tutorial 4, where we show that the EZ-Diffusion Model produces substantively identical drift-related conclusions to the computationally much more expensive full DDM.

## Hypothesis Testing

Because we fitted the model with `sample_prior = "yes"`, we can use `brms::hypothesis()` to test hypotheses about the condition effects via Savage-Dickey density ratios. Writing a hypothesis as an equality (e.g., `drift_word = drift_nonword`) asks how much the data changed our belief in *no difference*: the resulting `Evid.Ratio` compares the posterior to the prior density at a difference of zero, and its inverse is the Bayes Factor (BF) quantifying the evidence *against* equality. In other words, a BF of 10 means the data are ten times more likely under a model in which the two parameters differ than under one in which they are equal. As a rough guide, BFs above 3 indicate moderate evidence, above 10 strong evidence, and above 100 decisive evidence [@kass1995bayes]. All BFs reported in this tutorial follow this convention.

You can pass several hypotheses at once as a character vector, which keeps related tests together in one output table:

```{r}
#| label: t1-hypothesis
#| eval: true
hypothesis(fit_acc_ezdm, c(
  drift = "drift_stim_catword = drift_stim_catnonword",
  bound = "bound_conditionaccuracy = bound_conditionspeed"
))
```

The column to read is `Evid.Ratio`. For `bound` it is far below 1, so its inverse — the evidence against equality — is decisive (BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t1_bf_bound), "$\\infty$", signif(t1_bf_bound, 2))`): speed–accuracy emphasis unambiguously changes response caution.

For `drift` the test comes out the other way. The BF against equality is `r round(t1_bf_drift, 2)`, meaning the data favor *no difference* between words and nonwords by roughly `r round(1 / t1_bf_drift)` to 1. This does not contradict the parameter estimates — words do show nominally higher drift — but it tells us the collapsed word/nonword contrast is too coarse to separate drift reliably. Tutorial 4 revisits stimulus effects on drift at the frequency level, where the evidence against equality turns out to be decisive.

Two lessons follow, and both generalize beyond this dataset. Bayes Factors can quantify evidence *for* the absence of a difference, which a significance test cannot; and a selective influence test is only as sharp as the stimulus contrast you specify.

# Tutorial 2: Estimating Response Bias with the EZ-Diffusion Model (4par)

Tutorial 1 used accuracy coding, where "upper" means correct regardless of stimulus type. But what if we want to know whether participants are biased toward saying "word"? Response bias is a substantively important question in many domains: in lexical decision, word frequency creates an a priori expectation that biases responses toward "word"; in recognition memory, participants may adopt liberal or conservative response criteria; in clinical research, impulsive responding in ADHD may manifest as a shifted relative starting point rather than changed drift.

To estimate such biases you need two things: *response coding*, where "upper" always means a "word" response, and the 4-parameter EZ-Diffusion Model (`ezdm` 4par), which adds the relative starting point ($\zeta$) as a fourth parameter. The companion script for this tutorial is `scripts/12_tutorial2_ezdm_4par.R`, which also contains the simulated 4par validation.

## Model Specification

As introduced in the Data Preparation section, response coding changes the question the model answers — from "how quickly does evidence accumulate toward the *correct* answer?" to "how quickly does evidence accumulate toward saying *word*?" Drift is therefore positive for word stimuli and negative for nonwords. Bound and ndt retain their interpretations, but the key new parameter is the relative starting point $\zeta$: values above 0.5 indicate a tendency to say "word" before evidence accumulation has run its course, an *a priori response bias* that the accuracy-coded model could not detect.

The model object changes in two ways relative to Tutorial 1. Setting `version = "4par"` adds $\zeta$ to the estimated parameters, and `mean_rt` and `var_rt` now take a *pair* of column names rather than one each:

```{r}
#| label: t2-model
model_resp <- ezdm(
  mean_rt  = c("mean_rt_upper", "mean_rt_lower"),
  var_rt   = c("var_rt_upper", "var_rt_lower"),
  n_upper  = "n_upper",
  n_trials = "n_trials",
  version  = "4par"
)
```

That pairing is what makes the fourth parameter identifiable. With an unbiased starting point, responses at the two boundaries have the same mean and variance; a starting point closer to one boundary makes responses at that boundary faster and less variable than responses at the other. The 4par version recovers $\zeta$ from exactly this asymmetry, which is why it needs boundary-specific moments where the 3par version needed only one mean and one variance per cell.

The formula adds one line for the new parameter, and is otherwise the Tutorial 1 formula:

```{r}
#| label: t2-formula
formula_resp_ezdm <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

Note that $\zeta$ is written `zr` in the formula, and that it gets emphasis condition as a predictor: this asks whether participants shift their starting point when instructed to favor speed over accuracy.

## Model Fitting

Fitting uses the same `bmm()` call as Tutorial 1, with the response-coded summary statistics and the 4par model object substituted in. All sampler settings are unchanged, so we show only what differs:

```{r}
#| label: t2-fit
fit_resp_ezdm <- bmm(
  formula = formula_resp_ezdm,
  data    = data_resp_ezdm,
  model   = model_resp,
  file    = here("output", "fit_ezdm_lexical_resp")
)
```

## Model Evaluation

Convergence was adequate (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t2_rhat, 3)`). A posterior predictive check confirms adequate model fit (@fig-t2-ppcheck).

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the EZ-Diffusion 4par model fitted to the response-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_pp_check.pdf"))
```
