As expected, drift reverses by stimulus category: positive for word stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_word`, evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary) and negative for nonword stimuli ($\delta$ = `r t2_drift_nonword`, evidence accumulates toward the "nonword" boundary). This sign reversal is a direct consequence of response coding; the same underlying evidence accumulation process is now expressed relative to the "word" boundary rather than the "correct" boundary. The $\zeta$ estimates reveal a small starting-point shift: $\zeta$ = `r t2_zr_acc_ci` under accuracy emphasis and $\zeta$ = `r t2_zr_speed_ci` under speed emphasis. The accuracy-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_acc` suggests a slight bias toward saying "word," while the speed-emphasis estimate of `r t2_zr_speed` is close to unbiased. These values are consistent with the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis ($\zeta$ = 0.497 for accuracy, 0.476 for speed), confirming that this dataset shows only a very small a priori response bias (@fig-t2-params).

```{r}
#| label: fig-t2-params
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion 4par parameter estimates from the response-coded analysis. Left: Drift estimates by stimulus category, positive for word stimuli, negative for nonword stimuli. Middle: Bound estimates by emphasis condition. Right: Relative starting point by emphasis condition. Values near 0.5 indicate minimal response bias."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "12_resp_params.pdf"))
```

## Hypothesis Testing

Equality tests analogous to Tutorial 1 confirm the expected patterns. The Bayes Factors against zero drift for words (BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t2_bf_drift_word), "$\\infty$", signif(t2_bf_drift_word, 2))`) and for nonwords (BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t2_bf_drift_nw), "$\\infty$", signif(t2_bf_drift_nw, 2))`), and against equal bound across emphasis conditions (BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t2_bf_bound), "$\\infty$", signif(t2_bf_bound, 2))`), are all decisive. The selective influence pattern is robust to the change in response coding.

## Trial-Count Constraint

One practical limitation surfaced in this analysis, and it is worth dwelling on because it drives the rest of the tutorial. The `ezdm` 4par version requires enough trials on *both* boundaries in every cell. In this dataset, nonword stimuli under accuracy emphasis yield very few "word" responses — median 17 per cell, minimum 1 — which makes the variance estimate for the minority boundary unreliable. This is not a quirk of our preprocessing; it arises organically whenever a condition is easy enough that participants rarely err, and it is why we computed the 4par summary statistics with `method = "robust"` rather than `method = "mixture"`: the mixture method's EM step cannot converge on a cell containing a single observation.

The constraint is not merely a technical inconvenience. It points at a general limitation of summary-statistic approaches: when a cell contains very few responses on one boundary, the per-cell moments that the EZ-Diffusion Model requires stop being estimable, and no amount of care in preprocessing recovers them. Trial-level approaches sidestep the problem entirely, because they never form per-cell statistics — they evaluate a likelihood for each observation and borrow strength across participants through the hierarchical structure. We turn to the first of them next.

# Tutorial 3: Trial-Level Modeling with the Censored-Shifted Wald

So far, the EZ-Diffusion Model has worked with summary statistics — three numbers per cell. But what if we need to model individual RTs? Trial-level modeling preserves distributional information, allows trial-level predictors, and, critically, handles sparse cells through hierarchical shrinkage rather than requiring stable per-cell variance estimates. The companion script for this tutorial is `scripts/13_tutorial3_cswald.R`, which also contains the simulated Censored-Shifted Wald validation.

Evaluating the Wiener distribution's density involves an infinite series for every trial, which makes iterative model development with the full DDM expensive. The Censored-Shifted Wald sidesteps this with the single-boundary shifted Wald distribution introduced in the Background [@anders2016shifted; @heathcote2004fitting]: the simple version fits in about 4.5 hours on the present dataset rather than the better part of a day, and the approximation to the two-boundary DDM is close when error rates are low. That makes it a practical tool for developing and refining trial-level models before committing to the DDM's computational cost. The competing-risks version introduced below buys a different thing — an explicit account of error RTs and a relative starting point — and, as we report in the Cross-Approach Comparison, it costs about as much as the full DDM.

The `bmm` workflow itself is unchanged. Only two things differ from Tutorial 1: the model object (`cswald()` instead of `ezdm()`) and the data you pass it (trial-level RT and response columns instead of aggregated summary statistics).

## Model Specification: Simple Version

The *simple* version treats errors as censored observations, in the sense set out in the Background: each error tells the model only that the correct-boundary process had not finished by the observed RT. Because censored trials constrain the parameters less than completed ones, this version needs errors to stay reasonably rare. In the present dataset they do: accuracy-coded error rates range from 4% (nonwords, accuracy emphasis) to 19% (words, speed emphasis), within the ~20% guideline [@miller2018shifted].

The model object needs to know which column holds the RT and which holds the response, and which version to use:

```{r}
#| label: t3-model-simple
model_simple <- cswald(
  rt       = "rt",
  response = "response",
  version  = "simple"
)
```

Unlike `ezdm()`, which took four columns of pre-computed moments, `cswald()` takes the raw trial-level columns. The `response` column must contain the values `"upper"` and `"lower"`, identifying which boundary each trial reached — the coding we applied in the Data Preparation section. Under accuracy coding, `"upper"` means a correct response, so the censored trials are exactly the `"lower"` ones.

The formula is identical to Tutorial 1's, which is the point: the predictor structure you developed with the EZ-Diffusion Model transfers to the trial-level approach unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: t3-formula-simple
formula_simple <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

## Model Fitting: Simple Version

The `bmm()` call takes the cleaned trial-level data rather than the summary statistics; sampler settings are those from Tutorial 1.

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit-simple
fit_cswald_simple <- bmm(
  formula = formula_simple,
  data    = data_accuracy_clean,
  model   = model_simple,
  file    = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_simple")
)
```

## Model Evaluation: Simple Version

The model converged well (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t3_rhat_simple, 3)`), and the posterior predictive check (@fig-t3-ppcheck-simple) confirms adequate fit to the accuracy-coded RT distributions.

One point about scale is worth settling before you read the estimates. In the `bmm` parameterization, `cswald` returns bound on the full-boundary scale, the same scale as `ezdm` and `ddm`, so the three are directly comparable without rescaling — and empirically the simple version's bound estimates land close to the EZ-Diffusion Model's and to the published reference values (see Cross-Approach Comparison). That empirical agreement is not a guarantee, however. Of the three parameters, bound is the one the single-boundary approximation has the weakest claim on, because collapsing two boundaries into one is precisely an assumption about the boundaries; drift and ndt are the parameters this version recovers most dependably. Read a close match on bound as reassurance about this dataset, not as a property you can count on in general.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-ppcheck-simple
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) model fitted to the accuracy-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data. Dark lines show the observed RT distribution, light lines distributions simulated from the posterior."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "13_pp_check_simple.pdf"))
```

Substantively, the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) mirrors the EZ-Diffusion results. Bound is higher under accuracy emphasis (`r t3s_bound_acc`) than speed emphasis (`r t3s_bound_speed`), with decisive evidence against equality (BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t3_bf_bound), "$\\infty$", signif(t3_bf_bound, 2))`), while the small word–nonword drift difference ($\delta$ = `r t3s_drift_word` vs. `r t3s_drift_nonword`) again favors equality (BF = `r round(t3_bf_drift, 2)` against equality; see Tutorial 1). The agreement is worth pausing on: an approach that discards the two-boundary structure altogether recovers the same condition effects as one that models it.

## Model Specification: Competing-Risks Version

Where the simple version censors errors, the *competing-risks* (crisk) version models them explicitly: two accumulators race each other, one per response boundary, sharing a single non-decision time, and whichever finishes first produces the observed response. Nothing is left as a lower bound, which is what allows this version to estimate the relative starting point $\zeta$. We apply it to the response-coded data, where it can estimate $\zeta$ and handle the unbalanced boundary counts that limited the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach.

```{r}
#| label: t3-model-crisk
model_crisk <- cswald(
  rt       = "rt",
  response = "response",
  version  = "crisk"
)

formula_crisk <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + stim_cat + (0 + stim_cat | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

## Model Fitting and Evaluation: Competing-Risks Version

Fitting proceeds as before, with the response-coded data and the crisk model object:

```{r}
#| label: t3-fit-crisk
fit_cswald_crisk <- bmm(
  formula = formula_crisk,
  data    = data_response_clean,
  model   = model_crisk,
  file    = here("output", "fit_cswald_lexical_resp")
)
```

The crisk model also converged well (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t3_rhat_crisk, 3)`), and the posterior predictive check (@fig-t3-ppcheck-crisk) confirms adequate fit. Substantively, it recovers the drift sign reversal seen in the EZ-Diffusion 4par and estimates $\zeta$ close to 0.5 ($\zeta$ = `r t3c_zr_acc` under accuracy emphasis, `r t3c_zr_speed` under speed emphasis), consistent with both the EZ-Diffusion 4par results and the original analysis. Note that this version handled without complaint the sparse minority-boundary cells that forced the EZ-Diffusion 4par onto the robust aggregation method: because it evaluates a likelihood per trial rather than moments per cell, a cell with one "word" response is simply a cell with one observation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t3-ppcheck-crisk
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the Censored-Shifted Wald (competing-risks) model fitted to the response-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data. Dark lines show the observed RT distribution, light lines distributions simulated from the posterior."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "13_pp_check_crisk.pdf"))
```

## When to Use Which Version

Use the simple version when error rates are low (<20%) and your research question does not require estimating the relative starting point. Its estimates, including bound, are on a scale directly comparable to the other approaches, with drift and ndt recovered most reliably — and it is the only version of the Censored-Shifted Wald that is substantially cheaper than the full DDM (~4.5 h against 17–21 h here).

Use the crisk version when error rates are higher, when $\zeta$ is of interest, or when response coding is used. Two things are worth knowing before you commit to it. First, it costs about as much to fit as the full DDM (~18 h here), so it is a choice about what you want to estimate rather than a way to save time. Second, it systematically underestimates bound by approximately 10% relative to the DDM. That underestimation is an inherent property of the competing-risks approximation: two independent racing accumulators do not perfectly reproduce the dynamics of a single accumulator drifting between two boundaries.

In practice, the bound underestimation matters mainly when bound is interpreted on an absolute scale — for example, when estimates are compared against published values. The condition ordering of bound was preserved across approaches in our analyses (see Cross-Approach Comparison), but if your primary question concerns the precise magnitude of boundary effects, prefer the full DDM. For drift-focused questions, the Censored-Shifted Wald produces estimates that closely match the full DDM.

# Tutorial 4: Full DDM Likelihood Estimation

The Censored-Shifted Wald provides an efficient trial-level approach, but its single-boundary approximation does not fully capture the dynamics of the two-boundary decision process, as the systematic bound underestimation reflects. For confirmatory analyses, where you want the most accurate parameter estimates available, full DDM likelihood estimation is the gold standard: it models the complete RT distribution for both correct and error responses within a single likelihood, with neither approximation nor censoring.

In this tutorial we also increase model complexity, replacing the two-level stimulus category with the full four-level `freq` variable (high-frequency words, low-frequency words, very-low-frequency words, nonwords) on drift, matching the specification of @wagenmakers2008lexical. The companion scripts are `scripts/14_tutorial4_ddm.R` for the DDM fits and `scripts/15_cross_model_comparison.R` for the EZ-Diffusion comparison fits and figures.

Before comparing our estimates against published ones, one point about the scale of DDM parameters needs stating, because it silently invalidates comparisons that ignore it. DDM parameters are defined only relative to a scaling constant: multiplying drift, bound, and the diffusion noise $s$ by the same factor leaves the predicted data unchanged. `bmm` and Stan fix $s = 1$, whereas older software often used $s = 0.1$. Reference values drawn from that older literature must therefore be rescaled — by a factor of 10 — before they can be compared with `bmm` output. All reference values we quote below have been converted to $s = 1$.

## Model Specification

The model object is the simplest of the three. `ddm()` needs only the RT and response columns; there is no `version` argument, because the full DDM has one form, and $\zeta$ is included or omitted by whether the formula supplies a `zr` line.

```{r}
#| label: t4-model
model_ddm <- ddm(rt = "rt", response = "response")
```

For the accuracy-coded analysis, all drifts are positive: they measure evidence toward the correct boundary regardless of stimulus type. A consequence worth anticipating is that the drift rank order differs from the response-coded model. High-frequency words have the highest drift, but nonwords — which are relatively easy to reject — have higher drift than very-low-frequency words, which are difficult to recognize. The expected rank order from @wagenmakers2008lexical is HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > NW (2.64) > VLF (1.80).

```{r}
#| label: t4-formula-acc
formula_ddm_acc <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
)
```

For the response-coded analysis, drift sign reflects the stimulus: positive for words, where evidence accumulates toward the "word" boundary, and negative for nonwords. The expected values are HF (4.52) > LF (2.75) > VLF (1.80) > 0 > NW (−2.64). Adding a `zr` line lets $\zeta$ capture any bias toward saying "word"; the reference values suggest a very small shift between conditions ($\zeta$ = 0.497 accuracy, 0.476 speed).

```{r}
#| label: t4-formula-resp
formula_ddm_resp <- bmf(
  drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
  bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
  ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
  zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
)
```

## Model Fitting

We show the accuracy-coded call in full, since it is the last time the complete set of sampler settings appears; the response-coded fit differs only in its formula, data, and output file.

```{r}
#| label: t4-fit-acc
fit_ddm_acc <- bmm(
  formula = formula_ddm_acc,
  data    = data_accuracy_clean,
  model   = model_ddm,
  chains  = 5,
  cores   = 5,
  warmup  = 1000,
  iter    = 2000,
  backend = "cmdstanr",
  sample_prior = "yes",
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.90, max_treedepth = 12),
  file    = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_acc")
)
```

```{r}
#| label: t4-fit-resp
fit_ddm_resp <- bmm(
  formula = formula_ddm_resp,
  data    = data_response_clean,
  model   = model_ddm,
  file    = here("output", "fit_ddm_lexical_resp")
)
```

## Model Evaluation

Both DDM models converged (maximum $\hat{R}$ = `r round(t4_rhat_acc, 3)` for the accuracy-coded model, `r round(t4_rhat_resp, 3)` for the response-coded model). Posterior predictive checks (@fig-t4-ppcheck) confirm that the DDM captures the RT distributions well.

```{r}
#| label: fig-t4-ppcheck
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check for the DDM fitted to the accuracy-coded Wagenmakers et al. (2008) data."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "14_pp_check_acc.pdf"))
```

The accuracy-coded DDM recovers the expected drift rank ordering: HF (`r t4_drift_hf`) > NW (`r t4_drift_nw`) > LF (`r t4_drift_lf`) > VLF (`r t4_drift_vlf`). Bound is clearly higher under accuracy emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t4_bound_acc`) than speed emphasis ($\alpha$ = `r t4_bound_speed`), and ndt is estimated at $\tau$ = `r t4_ndt` s. The response-coded DDM estimates $\zeta$ close to 0.5 (`r t4_zr_acc` for accuracy, `r t4_zr_speed` for speed), consistent with the EZ-Diffusion 4par and Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) results.

We set `adapt_delta = 0.90` and `max_treedepth = 12` for both the Censored-Shifted Wald and the full DDM to reduce divergent transitions and max-treedepth warnings. If you fit trial-level DDMs of your own, start from these values rather than the `brms` defaults.

## Hypothesis Testing

As in the earlier tutorials, we quantify the evidence with equality tests. The Bayes Factor against equal bound across emphasis conditions (BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t4_bf_bound), "$\\infty$", signif(t4_bf_bound, 2))`) is decisive, reproducing the conclusion every previous tutorial reached.

More interesting is what the finer stimulus contrast does to the drift question. Tutorial 1 found that the collapsed word/nonword contrast *favored* equality of drift, and attributed this to the contrast being too coarse. The four-level frequency specification lets us check that diagnosis directly: the Bayes Factor against equal drift for high- and very-low-frequency words is decisive (BF = `r ifelse(is.infinite(t4_bf_drift), "$\\infty$", signif(t4_bf_drift, 2))`). Drift does vary with stimulus quality; Tutorial 1's null result was a property of how the stimulus contrast was specified, not of the parameter. This is worth carrying forward as a general lesson: a selective influence test is only as sharp as the contrast you give it.

## The EZ-Diffusion Model at the Same Specification

Given the computational cost of the full DDM, a natural question is whether the EZ-Diffusion Model can produce comparable results with the same model specification. To test this, we fitted the EZ-Diffusion Model with the identical four-level `freq` variable on drift, both accuracy-coded (3par) and response-coded (4par). Summary statistics were computed using the mixture method for the 3par model and the robust method for the 4par model, which avoids convergence issues in sparse cells (nonword stimuli under accuracy emphasis yield very few "word" responses).

```{r}
#| label: t4-ezdm-comparison
#| eval: false
# EZ-Diffusion 3par with freq (accuracy-coded); full code in scripts/15_cross_model_comparison.R
data_acc_ezdm_freq <- data_accuracy_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "3par",
                       method = "mixture", distribution = "exgaussian"),
    .by = c(id, condition, freq)
  )

fit_ezdm_freq <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
    bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
    ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id)
  ),
  data = data_acc_ezdm_freq,
  model = ezdm(mean_rt = "mean_rt", var_rt = "var_rt",
               n_upper = "n_upper", n_trials = "n_trials", version = "3par"),
  # ... same fitting settings as above
)

# EZ-Diffusion 4par with freq (response-coded)
data_resp_ezdm_freq <- data_response_clean |>
  summarize(
    ezdm_summary_stats(rt, response, version = "4par",
                       method = "robust", min_trials = 3),
    .by = c(id, condition, freq)
  )

fit_ezdm_resp_freq <- bmm(
  formula = bmf(
    drift ~ 0 + freq + (0 + freq | id),
    bound ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id),
    ndt   ~ 1 + (1 | id),
    zr    ~ 0 + condition + (0 + condition | id)
  ),
  data = data_resp_ezdm_freq,
  model = ezdm(mean_rt = c("mean_rt_upper", "mean_rt_lower"),
               var_rt = c("var_rt_upper", "var_rt_lower"),
               n_upper = "n_upper", n_trials = "n_trials", version = "4par"),
  # ... same fitting settings as above
)
```

Both EZ-Diffusion models converged in under three minutes, several hundred times faster than the full DDM. @fig-ezdm-vs-ddm compares the parameter estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ezdm-vs-ddm
#| fig-cap: "EZ-Diffusion vs. full DDM parameter estimates for the accuracy-coded analysis with four frequency levels on drift. Left: Drift estimates by frequency level. The EZ-Diffusion Model produces qualitatively identical rank orderings with slightly higher absolute values. Middle: Bound estimates by condition. The EZ-Diffusion Model underestimates bound relative to the full DDM, particularly under accuracy emphasis. Right: Non-decision time. The EZ-Diffusion Model estimates higher ndt than the full DDM. X markers show reference values from Wagenmakers et al. (2008)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_ezdm_vs_ddm_freq.pdf"))
```

The comparison reveals a systematic pattern. The EZ-Diffusion Model recovers the same drift rank ordering as the full DDM (HF > NW > LF > VLF in accuracy coding), but with drift estimates approximately `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% higher on average (ranging from `r t4_drift_pct_lo`% to `r t4_drift_pct_hi`% across frequency levels). The direction of this deviation is not fixed: relative to known generating values, EZ-Diffusion drift is *attenuated* at high values when trial-to-trial variability is present [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]; relative to the full DDM fitted to the same empirical data, as here, the estimates came out higher. What matters for practice is that condition differences in drift are amplified rather than reversed. The EZ-Diffusion Model underestimates bound relative to the full DDM, particularly under accuracy emphasis where the DDM uses the full RT distribution shape to inform boundary separation. Non-decision time is estimated higher by the EZ-Diffusion Model ($\tau$ = `r t4_ndt_ez` s) than the full DDM ($\tau$ = `r t4_ndt_ddm` s), likely because the EZ-Diffusion Model absorbs some decision-time variability into ndt. For the response-coded 4par model, the EZ-Diffusion Model also recovered the drift sign reversal (positive for words, negative for nonwords) and estimated $\zeta$ values consistent with the full DDM.

These results demonstrate that the EZ-Diffusion Model is not merely a rough screening tool but a viable estimation approach in its own right. When the research question centers on drift, which experimental factor affects which cognitive process, and in what direction, the EZ-Diffusion Model provides the same substantive conclusions as the full DDM at a fraction of the computational cost. This computational cost motivates the staged workflow described in the Practical Guidelines.

# Cross-Approach Comparison

Having applied all three DDM estimation approaches to the same empirical dataset, we can now evaluate a question that is difficult to answer without a unified framework: where the approaches agree, and where the approximations break down. Agreement validates the faster approaches against the gold-standard DDM; disagreement reveals where the computational savings come at a substantive cost.

## Accuracy-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-acc
#| fig-cap: "Cross-approach comparison of accuracy-coded parameter estimates. Panels show drift by word-frequency level, drift by collapsed stimulus category, bound by emphasis condition, and ndt. Colors distinguish the three estimation approaches; error bars show 95% credible intervals."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_accuracy.pdf"))
```

@fig-comparison-acc shows the accuracy-coded parameter estimates side by side. All three estimation approaches converge on the same substantive picture: emphasis condition clearly affects bound, drift differs strongly across word-frequency levels, and the collapsed word/nonword drift contrast is small in every approach. This convergence is reassuring; the conclusions hold regardless of whether we use summary statistics (EZ-Diffusion), a single-boundary approximation (Censored-Shifted Wald), or the full Wiener likelihood (DDM).

Where the approaches diverge, they diverge in absolute values, and in ways consistent with their known properties (@tbl-cross-model-acc reports the parameters all three share). The EZ-Diffusion Model produces higher drift estimates than the trial-level approaches — around `r t4_drift_pct_mean`% higher on the frequency scale, and more pronounced on the collapsed stimulus-category scale — mirroring the deviation documented in Tutorial 4.

For bound, the EZ-Diffusion and Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) estimates agree closely with each other and with the published reference values, while the full DDM estimates somewhat higher boundaries. The gap is most visible under accuracy emphasis, where the DDM draws on the full shape of the RT distribution rather than its first two moments. Ndt shows a clear ordering in the opposite direction: the EZ-Diffusion Model estimates higher ndt than the trial-level approaches, likely because it absorbs some decision-time variability that the distributional likelihoods capture directly.

All of these divergences concern the absolute parameter scale. On the two questions applied work actually asks — does the manipulation change the parameter, and do individuals differ from one another — the approaches agree. That distinction is developed in the Practical Guidelines.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cross-model-acc
#| tbl-cap: "Accuracy-coded parameter estimates (posterior mean [95% CrI], natural scale) for the parameters the three approaches share: bound by emphasis condition and ndt. Bound and ndt are back-transformed from the log link. Drift is compared in @fig-comparison-acc and @fig-ezdm-vs-ddm."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
.g3 <- function(fe, row, d = 2) fmt_est(exp(fe[row, c("Estimate", "Q2.5", "Q97.5")]), d)
cross_tab_acc <- tibble::tibble(
  Parameter = c("Bound, speed ($\\alpha$)", "Bound, accuracy ($\\alpha$)", "ndt ($\\tau$, s)"),
  `EZ-Diffusion`    = c(.g3(fe_t1,  "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t1,  "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t1,  "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Censored-Shifted Wald (simple)` = c(.g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t3s, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t3s, "ndt_Intercept", 3)),
  `Full DDM`        = c(.g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionspeed"), .g3(fe_t4a, "bound_conditionaccuracy"), .g3(fe_t4a, "ndt_Intercept", 3))
)
knitr::kable(cross_tab_acc, align = "lccc")
```

## Response-Coded Estimates

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison-resp
#| fig-cap: "Cross-approach comparison of response-coded parameter estimates. Left: Drift estimates by stimulus category. All three approaches show positive drift for words and negative drift for nonwords. Right: Relative starting point by emphasis condition. All three approaches estimate values close to 0.5. The Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) recovers the same drift sign reversal and near-unbiased starting point as the full DDM; its known underestimation of boundary separation is documented in the text below and the recovery study (Appendix)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "15_cross_model_response.pdf"))
```

The response-coded comparison (@fig-comparison-resp) evaluates whether the approaches agree on two key patterns: the drift sign reversal by stimulus category and the starting-point shift under speed emphasis. All three approaches recover the expected drift pattern, positive for word stimuli, negative for nonwords, confirming that the response-coding interpretation is robust across estimation approaches. The relative starting point $\zeta$ estimates are close to 0.5 across approaches and emphasis conditions, consistent with the small bias reported in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical analysis. The known bound underestimation of the Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk; see Tutorial 3) is visible in the boundary separation estimates; for boundary-focused questions, the full DDM remains preferable.

## Computational Cost

The fitting times on the present dataset span three orders of magnitude: 21 s to 2.5 min for the EZ-Diffusion fits, 4.5 h for the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple), 17.9 h for the Censored-Shifted Wald (competing-risks), and 17.5–20.6 h for the full DDM (wall-clock, five chains in parallel). Two features of this hierarchy matter for how the approaches should be used. First, the EZ-Diffusion Model provides in under a minute what takes the full DDM the better part of a day — for the accuracy-coded frequency specification, a factor of roughly 1,000. Second, the computational saving of the Censored-Shifted Wald is confined to its simple version: the competing-risks version costs essentially what the full DDM costs, so it should be chosen for what it estimates (a relative starting point at higher error rates), not for speed.

For research questions focused on drift, where all approaches agree closely, the EZ-Diffusion Model and the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple) are efficient alternatives. When the absolute values of bound or $\zeta$ are central — for example, when estimates are compared against published values — the full DDM is preferable, given the deviations documented above (amplified EZ-Diffusion drift differences, underestimated crisk bound).

# Practical Guidelines

## Things to Keep in Mind

Before the approach-specific recommendations, here are the requirements and conventions that apply whichever approach you use. Most of them have caused us or our students trouble at some point.

- **RTs must be in seconds.** `bmm` does not inspect or convert your RT scale, and the default priors on ndt assume seconds. If your data are in milliseconds, divide by 1000 before fitting.
- **The response column must contain `"upper"` and `"lower"`.** Decide deliberately which coding you want: accuracy coding (upper = correct) tests selective influence, response coding (upper = one specific response) reveals decision bias. They answer different questions from the same trials.
- **Bound and ndt are estimated on the log scale, and `zr` on the logit scale.** Back-transform with `exp()` and `plogis()` before interpreting or plotting anything, including credible-interval limits.
- **Parameters are defined only up to a scaling constant.** `bmm` fixes the diffusion noise at $s = 1$; older software often used $s = 0.1$. Rescale published values before comparing.
- **Check convergence before you interpret anything.** $\hat{R}$ below 1.01 and bulk ESS above 400 for every parameter you intend to report; `summary()` shows both.
- **Respect the trial-count minima** (@tbl-model-comparison): roughly 30 per cell for the EZ-Diffusion Model, which needs stable variance estimates, and roughly 50 for the trial-level approaches [@lerche2017trials; @boag2025expert].
- **Do not apply hard RT cutoffs.** Use `flag_contaminant_rts()` for trial-level data or `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture")` for aggregation, and let the mixture model handle contaminants.
- **ndt must fall below the fastest observed RT.** If ndt estimates sit suspiciously close to your minimum RT, read the Limitations section before interpreting them.

## When to Use Which Approach

The choice among the three estimation approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison) should be guided by the research question and stage of analysis:

- **EZ-Diffusion Model** (`ezdm`): Best for rapid exploration and designs with many conditions. Use 3par by default; 4par when starting-point bias is expected. Requires ~30 trials per cell for stable variance estimates [@lerche2017trials; @lerche2016model].

- **Censored-Shifted Wald** (`cswald`): Choose the version by what you need, not by speed. The simple version is the one that is genuinely cheap (~4.5 h here) and suits iterative trial-level model development at error rates below ~20%. The competing-risks version is what you need when error rates are higher or when the relative starting point is of interest; it yields DDM-comparable parameters apart from the bound underestimation noted in Tutorial 3, but it costs about as much to fit as the full DDM.

- **Full DDM** (`ddm`): Gold standard for confirmatory analysis. Plan for fitting times in the tens of hours (see @tbl-model-comparison).

These recommendations rest on a distinction worth making explicit, about what "accurate estimation" should mean in practice. Outside of simulations, the true absolute parameter values are unknown; there is no reference to recover. The criteria that carry applied work are therefore different: an estimation approach must detect differences between experimental conditions or groups, and it must separate individuals reliably [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. On both criteria the three approaches converge in our analyses; condition effects replicated across approaches (Cross-Approach Comparison), and subject-level estimates correlated highly with their generating values for all three (Appendix). The absolute-scale biases documented above are, in this sense, primarily a theoretical rather than a practical problem; they matter when estimates are compared against published values or interpreted as measurements on an absolute scale.

## Recommended Workflow

We recommend a staged workflow that exploits the computational hierarchy. This is an efficiency strategy, not a claim that staging produces a better final model: iterating on the predictor structure is cheap with the EZ-Diffusion Model and the Censored-Shifted Wald (simple), and, as the cross-approach comparison showed, the faster approaches are trustworthy guides for the drift-focused questions that dominate EAM applications. Divergences that follow the known patterns — amplified EZ-Diffusion drift differences, underestimated crisk bound — are expected by construction. A divergence *beyond* them, such as a reversed effect or a qualitatively different rank order, signals a potential problem (model misspecification, data-quality issues) worth investigating before you finalize the analysis.

1. **Explore with the EZ-Diffusion Model** (`ezdm`): Rapidly screen condition effects on drift and identify which experimental factors influence which parameters.

2. **Develop with the Censored-Shifted Wald, simple version** (`cswald`): Move to trial-level modeling here, where each iteration still costs hours rather than a day. Refine the predictor structure, test different random-effects specifications, and evaluate prior sensitivity. Note that this stage is only available to you if error rates are below ~20%; above that, development has to happen at competing-risks or full-DDM cost.

3. **Confirm with the full DDM** (`ddm`): Fit the final model specification using the full DDM likelihood for confirmatory analysis.

4. **Cross-validate**: Compare Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM estimates as a robustness check.

Throughout all stages, preprocess data using `ezdm_summary_stats(method = "mixture")` for `ezdm` fitting or `flag_contaminant_rts()` for trial-level contaminant detection. Do not apply hard RT cutoffs when using the mixture method.

Adequate trial counts are essential for all approaches (see @tbl-model-comparison). The EZ-Diffusion Model is particularly sensitive because it relies on variance estimates, which stabilize more slowly than means [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion; @lerche2017trials]. For the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM, @boag2025expert recommend at least 50 trials per condition for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.

## Prior Selection

All tutorials used `bmm`'s default priors, Cauchy(0, 1) on drift, Normal(0, 0.5) on bound (log link), Normal(-1.5, 0.5) on ndt (log link), which are moderately informative and calibrated for typical data. Defaults can be inspected via `default_prior(formula, data, model)` and overridden using `brms::prior()`:

```{r}
#| label: priors-custom
custom_priors <- prior(normal(0, 2), class = "b", dpar = "drift") +
  prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", dpar = "bound")
```

When specifying custom priors, verify that they generate plausible RT data with a prior predictive check, fit with `sample_prior = "only"` and inspect `pp_check()`, and tighten them if the predictions are implausible.

## Common Issues and Troubleshooting

Convergence problems respond to the standard `brms`/Stan remedies: raise `adapt_delta`, increase iterations, simplify the random-effects structure, or fix $\zeta$ at 0.5. See the `brms` documentation for details [@burkner2017brms]. Two issues are EAM-specific. The mixture EM in `ezdm_summary_stats()` and `flag_contaminant_rts()` stops at its default iteration cap in a few percent of cells; the first function then silently returns the robust statistics (`contaminant_prop = NA`) and the second returns `NA` probabilities, which a `filter()` on the probability drops together with the entire cell. Pass `maxit = 500` and check that no cell has `NA` in `contaminant_prop`. The other issue: if the Censored-Shifted Wald and full DDM disagree on bound, this is the expected underestimation (see Tutorial 3), not a fitting problem; use the full DDM when boundary separation is the primary research question.

# Summary and Discussion

This tutorial applied three approaches for estimating DDM parameters — the EZ-Diffusion Model, the Censored-Shifted Wald, and full DDM likelihood estimation — to empirical data from a classic lexical decision experiment, all within `bmm`. Four tutorials ran the same three-step workflow with a different model object each time, which is the practical point of a unified interface: what you learn about specifying and interpreting one approach transfers to the others.

Three themes ran through them. First, data preprocessing is a quantifiable necessity rather than housekeeping, and the mixture-model approach consistently outperforms hard cutoffs. Second, the three approaches form a computational hierarchy that supports staged analysis — though, as the timings showed, that hierarchy has only two genuinely distinct speed tiers, since the competing-risks Censored-Shifted Wald costs what the full DDM costs. Third, response coding determines what questions a model can answer: accuracy coding tests selective influence, response coding reveals decision bias, and the EZ-Diffusion 4par approach runs into practical constraints when boundary trial counts are unbalanced.

## The Hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model as a Viable Alternative

The cross-approach comparison carries one practical message beyond the staged workflow. For drift-related research questions, the hierarchical EZ-Diffusion Model produced substantively identical conclusions to the full DDM at more than 1,000× lower computational cost.

Within `bmm`, the EZ-Diffusion Model is no longer the standalone calculator originally proposed by @wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion. It is a full Bayesian hierarchical model, with population-level effects, arbitrary predictor structures via `bmf()`, and shrinkage across participants — which addresses its two main historical criticisms: contaminant sensitivity, handled here by the mixture preprocessing, and the absence of hierarchical structure [@ratcliff2008ez; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. Recasting the EZ-Diffusion equations as a probabilistic proxy likelihood is what makes this possible, and provides its theoretical justification [@chavez2025ez]. Prior simulation work also reports statistical power for detecting condition effects comparable to or higher than the full DDM's [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]; we did not re-evaluate that result, but it is consistent with the convergence we observed.

Two qualifications remain. First, clean convergence in sparse cells reflects hierarchical shrinkage: estimates for cells with only a handful of minority-boundary responses are pulled toward the group-level prior and should be read as regularized rather than data-driven. Second, when the research question concerns the shape of the RT distribution (e.g., leading-edge effects, the relative speed of errors) or the absolute values of bound or ndt, the full DDM remains the appropriate choice, with the Censored-Shifted Wald as the trial-level middle ground. For the more common targets, condition effects and individual differences, the estimation biases of the faster approaches are a theoretical rather than a practical concern [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez].

## Limitations

Within the scope defined in the Introduction — the simple DDM framework, two-choice tasks — several aspects were not demonstrated. We did not show between-trial variability parameters ($s_v$, $s_\zeta$, $s_\tau$), which can improve fit but create identifiability challenges [@luken2025identifiability; @boag2025expert]; if you need the full seven-parameter DDM, consider alternatives such as HDDM [@wiecki2013hddm] or a custom Stan implementation. We also did not cover formal model comparison; bridge sampling and leave-one-out cross-validation are available via `brms` but were beyond the present scope.

One of these omissions deserves more than a mention, because it affects how the ndt estimates in this tutorial should be read. Trial-to-trial variability in non-decision time ($s_\tau$) has a specific consequence for the two trial-level approaches: both the shifted Wald likelihood and the Wiener likelihood require ndt to fall below the fastest observed RT. When ndt in fact varies from trial to trial but is modeled as constant, its estimate is pinned to the leading edge of the RT distribution, and the remaining parameters can absorb the misfit [@miller2018shifted]. This is a plausible contributor to the ndt ordering we observed in the Cross-Approach Comparison, where the trial-level approaches estimated lower ndt than the EZ-Diffusion Model.

The three approaches are not equally exposed. A forthcoming `bmm` extension relaxes the constraint for the Censored-Shifted Wald by adding an explicit uniform trial-to-trial ndt component (`sndt`) to the likelihood. The full DDM in `bmm` cannot be extended the same way: it relies on Stan's internal `wiener_lpdf()`, which provides no term for non-decision-time variability, and adding one requires the seven-parameter DDM, whose across-trial convolutions are prohibitively slow for hierarchical Bayesian estimation. The EZ-Diffusion Model is comparatively robust, because it recovers ndt from the mean rather than the minimum RT, so realistic trial-to-trial variability leaves its parameter recovery largely intact [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion]. This is one of the few respects in which the fastest approach is also the most forgiving.

# References

# Evaluating the Preprocessing Methods {.appendix}

The Data Preprocessing section recommended the mixture method with an ex-Gaussian core distribution, the robust method as a fallback, and no hard pre-filtering. This appendix reports the evidence for those recommendations. The companion scripts are `scripts/02_simulation_contaminant_methods.R` for the Monte Carlo study, `scripts/02b_simulation_validation_ezdm.R` for its validation with hierarchical `ezdm()` fits, `scripts/10_tutorial0_data_preprocessing.R` for the contaminant-bias demonstration, and `scripts/10b_preprocessing_comparison.R` for the systematic comparison of flagging settings.

## Comparing Preprocessing Methods

The Monte Carlo study, run with `SimDesign` [@chalmers2020simdesign] and structured after the ADEMP framework (aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, performance measures; @morris2019simulation), simulated 50 participants who completed 50 or 200 trials in an easy and a hard condition (population drift 2.5 and 1.0; bound 1.5 and ndt 0.3 s, the same in both conditions; participant-level random effects on all three) and replaced 0, 2, 5, or 10% of each participant's trials per condition with contaminants from one of three processes that differ in their psychological source and in how far they overlap the core RT distribution: *fast guesses*, uniform RTs between 100 ms and the participant's ndt with responses at chance [@ratcliff2008ez], which lie entirely outside the core and are therefore the case the mixture model assumes (a contaminant component that the core distribution does not reach); *delayed start-ups*, a delay uniformly distributed between 0 and 2 s added to a genuine decision RT, the convention since @ratcliff2002estimating that also underlies the original validation of robust-EZ [@wagenmakers2008extensions]; and *informationless responses*, trials redrawn from a diffusion process with zero drift [@vandekerckhove2008bayesian; @chavez2026robust], whose RTs overlap the core completely and whose accuracy is at chance. The estimand — the quantity each method is scored against — was not the summary statistics themselves, because the clean sample moments are a target the plain moments (`simple`) hit by construction and the median cannot, but the generating drift, bound, and ndt of every participant × condition cell, obtained by passing each method's statistics through the closed-form EZ equations [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion], the same equations `ezdm()` uses, together with two practical estimands: the easy − hard drift difference and the correlation between participant-level estimates and their generating values. Bias and RMSE were computed over 200 replications, and an oracle that computes the plain moments after perfect contaminant exclusion marks the best any flagging method could achieve. On clean data the mixture method recovers all three parameters with negligible bias, whereas the median and IQR-based statistics inflate drift by about 10% (+0.27 in the easy and +0.12 in the hard condition) and deflate bound by about 10% while leaving ndt essentially intact (−0.002 to −0.019 s), so that the drift contrast is inflated by the same proportion (+0.15 on a true difference of 1.5). The lognormal and inverse-Gaussian cores are misspecified for diffusion RTs: even without contamination they flag about 2% of trials as contaminants and return drift and bound biases as large as the robust method's, which is why the ex-Gaussian is the default core.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simulation-methods
#| fig-cap: "Signed bias in the EZ-Diffusion parameters recovered by each preprocessing method (estimate − generating value; 200 replications, 200 trials per cell) by contaminant process (columns), parameter (rows), and contamination rate. Solid lines: easy condition; dashed lines: hard condition. The oracle computes the plain moments after perfect contaminant exclusion. Points are means over participants and replications; Monte Carlo standard errors are at most 0.03."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "02_method_comparison.pdf"))
```

@fig-simulation-methods shows the bias in the three parameters under contamination, and @tbl-simulation-practical the practical estimands at 5% contamination with 200 trials. Three patterns organize the results. First, whether a method helps depends on where the contaminants sit. Under 5% delayed start-ups the plain moments break down (drift −0.61, bound +0.46, ndt −0.14 in the easy condition; drift contrast −0.49) and both alternatives hold: the mixture method flags most delays and keeps every parameter within about 0.1, and the robust statistics stay within their fixed offset. Under fast guesses the mixture flags four fifths of them in the easy condition (an estimated 4.1% of a true 5%) but only a quarter in the hard condition (1.2%), where its ex-Gaussian core is wide enough to absorb them; under informationless responses it flags almost none (0.2–0.5%) and returns what the plain moments return. Second, contaminants reach the EZ equations through two channels, the RT distribution and the proportion correct, and no summary-statistic method corrects the second: chance-accuracy trials lower the proportion correct whatever happens to the RTs, and at the accuracy level of an easy condition this accuracy channel dominates: with 5% fast guesses or informationless responses the easy-condition drift is attenuated by −0.36 and −0.46 for the plain moments and by −0.23 and −0.37 for the mixture method, so the drift contrast shrinks even after every RT-based correction, whereas the robust statistics lose less (−0.06 and −0.10), partly because their intrinsic drift inflation offsets the attenuation. Because all three processes bite harder in the easy condition, they also manufacture condition differences in bound and ndt that do not exist in the generating model (bound +0.46 versus +0.18 for the plain moments under delays). Third, participant-level correlations are far less affected than mean levels: with 200 trials the drift correlations stay at .89 or above for the mixture and robust methods under every process at 5%, and only the plain moments fall to .76–.80 under delays and informationless responses. Hard pre-filtering at 150 ms and 5 s removed only the fast guesses below 150 ms and left the other processes untouched; at the ndt of 0.3 s used here it harmed no method and helped only modestly (the plain moments' easy-condition drift bias under fast guesses fell from −0.36 to −0.26), though fixed cutoffs truncate legitimate responses once they approach the leading edge of the distribution [@ulrich1994effects]. With 50 trials per cell the picture is the same but every estimate is noisier (drift correlations of .6–.9, ndt correlations of .3–.7). Fitting `bmm`'s hierarchical `ezdm()` to one dataset per process reproduces the closed-form pattern: posterior means differ from the closed-form estimates by at most 0.05 for drift and 0.01 s for ndt, and by more only where hierarchical shrinkage pulls in a badly inflated bound (0.15 for the plain moments under delayed start-ups); the ranking of the methods is unchanged (`scripts/02b_simulation_validation_ezdm.R`). Two implementation details matter in practice: the mixture EM was run with `maxit = 500`, under which it converged in more than 99.8% of cells, because with the default cap of 100 iterations it stops early in roughly 4–7% of 200-trial cells and `ezdm_summary_stats()` then silently substitutes the robust statistics (recognizable by `contaminant_prop = NA`); and in about one cell in 10^5^ the ex-Gaussian fit ran away to an implausible solution, which the study screened out by requiring the fitted mean to lie within the observed RT range.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-simulation-practical
#| tbl-cap: "Practical estimands at 5% contamination with 200 trials per cell (200 replications): bias and RMSE of the easy − hard drift difference (true difference ≈ 1.5), correlations between participant-level estimates and generating values (drift by condition; bound and ndt averaged over conditions), and the proportion of trials the mixture method flagged as contaminants (mixture only; true rate 5%). Oracle: plain moments after perfect contaminant exclusion."
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
sim_sum <- readr::read_csv(here("data", "simulation_preprocessing_summary.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)
sim_tab <- sim_sum |>
  dplyr::filter(p_contam == 0.05, n_trials == 200,
                method %in% c("Simple", "Robust", "Mixture (ex-Gaussian)",
                              "Oracle (perfect exclusion)"),
                measure %in% c("bias_effect", "rmse_effect", "cor_drift",
                               "cor_bound", "cor_ndt", "pi_c")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(key = dplyr::if_else(condition == "All", measure,
                                     paste(measure, condition, sep = "_"))) |>
  dplyr::select(process, method, key, value) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = key, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Process = stringr::str_replace(process, " \\(.*\\)", ""),
    Method = dplyr::recode(method, "Mixture (ex-Gaussian)" = "Mixture",
                           "Oracle (perfect exclusion)" = "Oracle"),
    `Drift effect: bias (RMSE)` = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", bias_effect, rmse_effect),
    `r drift, easy` = sprintf("%.2f", cor_drift_Easy),
    `r drift, hard` = sprintf("%.2f", cor_drift_Hard),
    `r bound` = sprintf("%.2f", (cor_bound_Easy + cor_bound_Hard) / 2),
    `r ndt` = sprintf("%.2f", (cor_ndt_Easy + cor_ndt_Hard) / 2),
    Flagged = dplyr::if_else(is.na(pi_c_Easy), "",
                             sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * (pi_c_Easy + pi_c_Hard) / 2))
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(Process = dplyr::if_else(duplicated(Process), "", Process))
knitr::kable(sim_tab, align = "llcccccc")
```

@chavez2026robust ask a complementary question with the plain moments and the median/IQR statistics but without a mixture method, tracing contamination through to hypothesis tests on drift effects. The two studies agree where they overlap: the plain moments break down under contamination, contamination attenuates drift effects toward zero and thereby inflates Type II error rates, and the damage is worst when drift is high and RTs fast, so that easy tasks are the ones where preprocessing matters most — the opposite of the intuition that clean, high-accuracy data need less care. Their conclusion that the robust variant costs nothing on clean data holds for their estimand, tests on drift effects, and not for absolute parameter values, where it costs about 10% of drift and bound.

## Validation Against Published Exclusion Criteria

The simulation above establishes that the mixture method works under controlled conditions where the ground truth is known. Whether it also works on real data, where the true contamination rate is unknown, is a separate question. We can address it by validating the method against the exclusion criteria used in the original @wagenmakers2008lexical study, which removed trials with RT < 180 ms or RT > 3000 ms — a standard hard-cutoff approach.

Applying `flag_contaminant_rts()` to the full dataset, including the trials the original study excluded, the mixture model catches 91.5% of the trials the hard cutoffs flagged. The 14 missed trials fall just below the 0.5 threshold, with contaminant probabilities of 0.30–0.49, and are borderline cases near the cutoff boundaries. More importantly, the mixture model additionally flags 143 trials *within* the 180 ms–3 s range that the hard cutoffs miss entirely: trials with abnormally long RTs (median 2.1 s) that the mixture model identifies as distributional outliers from the shape of the RT distribution. The mixture approach is therefore strictly more informative than hard cutoffs, recovering nearly all the same exclusions while detecting additional outliers that fixed thresholds cannot reach.

# Parameter Recovery on Simulated Data {.appendix}

## When to Assess Parameter Recovery

Parameter recovery is not mandatory for every analysis, but it is informative as part of a principled Bayesian workflow — particularly when you apply a model to a new design for the first time, when trial counts per cell are unusual or unbalanced, or when individual-level estimates will feed into correlations. Beyond validating a given design, recovery simulations can inform experimental planning: by systematically varying the number of participants or trials, you can determine what your design needs to achieve acceptable recovery for the parameters you care about. For the EZ-Diffusion Model a single recovery run costs minutes, so there is little reason not to do it; for the trial-level approaches, budget the fitting times reported in @tbl-model-comparison.

The study reported here verifies that the three `bmm` DDM estimation approaches produce reliable estimates, and complements the extensive parameter recovery literature for DDMs [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @lerche2016model]. The companion script is `scripts/21_appendix_parameter_recovery.R`.

## Simulation Design

We generated data from a DDM with known parameters (drift: 2.5 for easy, 1.0 for hard; bound: 1.5; ndt: 0.3; $\zeta$: 0.5) for 50 participants, each completing 200 trials per condition. Individual-level parameters were drawn from normal distributions around the population means (see `scripts/20_prepare_simulated_data.R` for details). We then fitted the EZ-Diffusion 3par, Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk), and full DDM to these data following the same `bmm` workflow used in the tutorials. We set two a-priori criteria for successful recovery: at the group level, the 95% credible interval for each parameter should contain its generating value (calibration); at the subject level, true and recovered values should correlate at $r > .70$, the conventional benchmark for treating a measure as a reliable individual-difference index. Of the two, the subject-level criterion is the practically more important one: absolute calibration can only be evaluated in simulations, whereas ordering individuals correctly is what applied uses of DDM parameters, as predictors, covariates, or outcomes, rely on.

## Group-Level Recovery

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-group
#| fig-cap: "Group-level parameter recovery. Points indicate posterior means for each estimation approach; error bars show 95% credible intervals. Dashed lines mark the true generating values. All three approaches recover drift and ndt accurately. The Censored-Shifted Wald (crisk) shows the expected underestimation of bound (see Tutorial 3)."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_group.pdf"))
```

All three estimation approaches recovered the generating parameters within their 95% credible intervals (@fig-recovery-group). Drift and ndt estimates were highly consistent across approaches; bound showed the expected crisk underestimation (see Tutorial 3).

## Subject-Level Recovery

Beyond group-level means, we evaluated whether the models recover individual differences by correlating true participant-level parameters with their posterior estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-subject
#| fig-cap: "Subject-level parameter recovery. Each point represents one participant's recovered posterior mean plotted against its true generating value (x-axis); vertical bars show the 95% credible interval of the individual-level posterior. High correlations indicate that the estimation approaches preserve the rank ordering of individual differences. Columns show drift (easy and hard conditions), bound, and ndt; rows show the three estimation approaches."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_subject.pdf"))
```

Subject-level correlations between true and recovered parameters were high across all estimation approaches (@fig-recovery-subject), ranging from $r$ = `r recovery_r_min` to `r recovery_r_max` (median $r$ = `r recovery_r_median`). These strong correlations indicate that the hierarchical structure in `bmm` preserves individual differences while borrowing strength across participants, an essential property for studies that use DDM parameters as individual difference measures. The results are consistent with published recovery studies and confirm that all three `bmm` estimation approaches produce reliable estimates at both the group and individual level under controlled conditions.
